SIRNET: Causal Adaptation of Pretrained Embeddings for Semiparametric Treatment-Effect Estimation Under Surrogacy

 

Lei Shi          Qiuran Lyu Adobe Research leis@adobe.com          Division of Biostatistics UC Berkeley qiuran_lyu@berkeley.edu

Abstract

Modern experiments increasingly produce rich post-treatment objects—such as text, images, and video—that may provide early surrogate signals for outcomes that are delayed, expensive, or observed only for a subset of participants. A pretrained encoder can turn such an object into a strong generic embedding, but the embedding is not trained for the estimation tasks required by a causal estimator and may emphasize information irrelevant to the causal target. We propose SIRNET, a Surrogate-Informed Representation adaptation framework for neural-NETwork-based causal estimation in the presence of unstructured post-treatment surrogates. Starting from pretrained surrogate embeddings, SIRNET learns a shared adapter jointly for outcome prediction, treatment propensity, and arm-specific surrogate marginalization, beyond the generic pretraining objective. The resulting covariate and surrogate representations provide a common interface for these nuisance tasks. The final treatment-effect estimate and confidence interval are obtained from cross-fitted orthogonal scores that attain the semiparametric efficiency bound under the stated nuisance-rate conditions. We also validate SIRNET’s performance in synthetic and semisynthetic experiments, as well as the Anti-Amyloid in Asymptomatic Alzheimer’s Disease (A4) trial, using frozen pretrained brain-MRI embeddings as surrogates for a long-term outcome.

1 Introduction

Background.

Many modern experiments collect rich post-treatment objects for every unit but observe the primary outcome only later or only for a costly subset. These objects can serve as early signals for the primary outcome, and are referred to as surrogates (Prentice, 1989; Athey et al., 2026). In an online education experiment (Kestin et al., 2025; Pardos and Bhandari, 2024), for example, treatment may be an AI-assisted feedback tool, the surrogate an essay written during the course, and the primary outcome a final standardized test score that could be missing for students who leave the online course or skip testing. In a clinical trial, treatment may be a new therapy, early MRI scans may be surrogates, and a later clinical or imaging endpoint may be unavailable because of dropout, death, or a missed visit (Sperling et al., 2014). Such text, image, and multimodal objects are far richer than classical scalar surrogates. Although pretrained encoders can summarize them effectively for their source task, the resulting embeddings do not necessarily emphasize the information needed for causal estimation. In particular, generic embedding directions can be predictive of visual or linguistic content while being irrelevant, or even distracting, for the nuisance functions of a causal estimator (Veitch et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2019).

This paper studies how to adapt pretrained embeddings of unstructured surrogates in a single sample with partially observed outcomes: all units in one sample have baseline covariates XX, treatment WW, and a post-treatment object SS, but the outcome YY is partially observed, indicated by a response variable RR. The goal is the average treatment effect

τ=𝔼⁡[Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)].\tau=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)].

The challenge for this problem is three-fold. First, the surrogate SS is post-treatment: S=S⁡(W)S=S(W) is the realized potential surrogate under the unit’s assigned arm. Hence, estimators that condition on the observed (Xi,Si)(X_{i},S_{i}) without accounting for the arm-specific potential-surrogate distribution will be biased. Second, the surrogates are unstructured and high-dimensional. A pretrained embedding SS can be predictive in general while retaining or emphasizing variation irrelevant to causal effect estimation. Third, given that the outcome is only partially observed, the surrogate can be informative both for predicting the outcome and for modeling its observation. Without properly accounting for these factors, treatment-effect estimates can be biased and inefficient.

Contributions.

In this paper, we propose SIRNET, a Surrogate-Informed Representation Network for treatment-effect estimation that addresses these challenges. Our central claim is that multitask causal representation adaptation from pretrained embeddings for unstructured surrogates can improve nuisance estimation for a semiparametric estimator. SIRNET learns a shared adaptation of the baseline covariates and post-treatment embeddings for the nuisance functions required by the orthogonal score. Its outcome, treatment, labeling, and marginal-outcome heads train that adaptation jointly, so the learned coordinates are selected for the causal nuisance tasks rather than the generic pretraining objective. The final treatment-effect estimate is obtained from cross-fitted orthogonal scores, not a direct neural-network contrast, yielding robustness to model misspecification and statistically valid inference under certain conditions. From a theoretical perspective, we also give sufficient conditions connecting representation-level nuisance approximation to existing semiparametric inference theory. Moreover, we validate SIRNET using extensive synthetic and semisynthetic experiments, as well as a real-world study on the Anti-Amyloid in Asymptomatic Alzheimer’s Disease (A4) study (Sperling et al., 2014), which is a Phase 3 randomized trial of solanezumab in cognitively unimpaired older adults with elevated brain amyloid. The experiments demonstrate improvements in nuisance learning and causal estimation precision compared with baseline methods that do not leverage such surrogate-informed representation adaptation.

2 Related Work

Surrogate endpoints and the surrogate index.

Prentice (1989) formalised the notion of a surrogate endpoint as one that fully mediates the treatment effect on the primary outcome, which is called the Prentice criterion. Subsequent work proposed alternative notions and validation criteria, including the proportion of treatment effect explained (Freedman et al., 1992), individual- and trial-level measures of surrogacy (Buyse and Molenberghs, 1998), and causal formulations based on potential outcomes and principal stratification (Frangakis and Rubin, 2002). More recently, Athey et al. (2026) propose the surrogate index: a scalar summary g^​(S)\hat{g}(S) trained on a reference population where YY is observed, used as a proxy for YY in a target experiment. Kallus and Mao (2025) study the role of surrogates in the efficient estimation of treatment effects with limited outcome data, which motivates our setup, and derive the efficient influence function for this setting. But the estimator is not directly equipped to adapt generic embeddings through multitask nuisance learning. SIRNET builds on their work by using the efficient score as its estimation target and adapting pretrained embeddings for all nuisance functions required by the score.

Partially observed outcomes and missing-data methods.

Estimating treatment effects when the outcome is missing for some units is a classical problem. Complete-case analysis and regression imputation works only under strong assumptions (Little and Rubin, 2019). Inverse-probability-weighted (IPW) estimators (Rosenbaum and Rubin, 1983) reweight the complete cases by the reciprocal of the observed-outcome probability Pr⁡(R=1∣W,X)\Pr(R=1\mid W,X). Doubly robust (DR) augmented-IPW estimators (Bang and Robins, 2005) are consistent if either the outcome model or the selection model is correct. Kallus and Mao (2025) derive the efficient influence function for treatment effect estimation with limited outcome data, where the surrogate SS can enter both the outcome model and the selection model. They also show that the efficient score strictly dominates the XX-only AIPW estimator whenever SS is informative about YY conditional on XX. SIRNET uses this efficient score as its estimation target, with a deep network providing the nuisance estimates.

Deep learning for treatment-effect estimation.

Several neural architectures use deep learning to improve treatment-effect estimation. Early work by Johansson et al. (2016) framed counterfactual prediction as a representation-learning problem. Building on this idea, Shalit et al. (2017) proposed TARNet and CFRNet, which learn a shared representation before splitting into treatment-specific outcome heads. Related approaches use alternative representation-learning objectives, including preservation of local similarity (Yao et al., 2018), propensity-matched minibatch construction (Schwab et al., 2018), and adversarial counterfactual generation (Yoon et al., 2018). Shi et al. (2019) augment a shared outcome representation with a treatment-propensity head and targeted regularisation designed specifically for treatment-effect estimation. More recently, architectures such as FlexTENet allow both shared and treatment-specific components (Curth and Van der Schaar, 2021). These methods focus on covariates that are pre-treatment but do not address post-treatment surrogates. A separate line of work learns representations of short-run surrogates for long-run effect estimation. Cheng et al. (2021) learn a sequential surrogate representation designed to accommodate time-varying confounding under a temporal-unconfoundedness assumption. Cai et al. (2024) instead learn latent surrogate representations from observed surrogates and proxies of potentially unobserved surrogates using an identifiable variational autoencoder. These works share SIRNET’s motivation of tailoring representations to the causal target rather than using raw surrogate measurements unchanged, but address different identification problems and inferential targets.

3 Setup and Methodology Foundation

3.1 Setup

For units i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, let

Oi=(Xi,Wi,Si,Ri,Ri​Yi)O_{i}=(X_{i},W_{i},S_{i},R_{i},R_{i}Y_{i})

denote the observed data. Here Xi∈𝒳X_{i}\in\mathcal{X} are pre-treatment covariates, Wi∈{0,1}W_{i}\in\{0,1\} is a binary treatment, SiS_{i} is the post-treatment object, and Ri∈{0,1}R_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether the primary outcome is observed. Our methodology development relies on the following assumptions.

Assumption 1 (Ignorability and overlap).

Treatment satisfies

(Yi​(1),Yi​(0),Si​(1),Si​(0))⟂Wi|Xi,(Y_{i}(1),Y_{i}(0),S_{i}(1),S_{i}(0))\perp W_{i}\mid X_{i},

and there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that ϵ<e⁡(Xi)<1−ϵ\epsilon<e(X_{i})<1-\epsilon, where e⁡(x)=ℙ⁡(Wi=1∣Xi=x)e(x)=\mathbb{P}(W_{i}=1\mid X_{i}=x).

Assumption 1 is standard in causal inference. It requires that the treatment assignment is independent of the potential outcomes and potential surrogates, given the pre-treatment covariates, which usually holds in randomized experiments. The overlap condition ensures that there is a positive probability of receiving either treatment for all values of the covariates, which is necessary for estimating the treatment effect across the entire population. These are standard assumptions in causal inference with surrogate outcomes (Athey et al., 2026; Chen and Ritzwoller, 2023), and they are necessary for identifying the average treatment effect.

Assumption 2 (Conditional missing at random).

Outcome labeling is conditionally ignorable:

Ri⟂Yi|Wi,Xi,Si,R_{i}\perp Y_{i}\mid W_{i},X_{i},S_{i},

with ϵ<r⁡(Wi,Xi,Si)<1−ϵ\epsilon<r(W_{i},X_{i},S_{i})<1-\epsilon, where r⁡(w,x,s)=ℙ⁡(Ri=1∣Wi=w,Xi=x,Si=s)r(w,x,s)=\mathbb{P}(R_{i}=1\mid W_{i}=w,X_{i}=x,S_{i}=s).

The second assumption is the key identifying condition for partial outcome observation (Kallus and Mao, 2025). This assumption is more debatable in general because it is not guaranteed by randomization. It requires that the outcome observation mechanism is independent of the outcome itself, conditional on the treatment, covariates, and surrogate. It is an extension of the conditional missing at random (MAR) assumption in missing data literature (Little and Rubin, 2019), which allows for the outcome to be missing in a way that depends on observed variables. One argument for its plausibility in the presence of surrogates is that the surrogate SS is a rich post-treatment object that may capture information relevant to both the outcome and the outcome observation. Without it, the effect is generally not identifiable and a separate sensitivity analysis framework is needed to address the challenge, which is beyond the scope of the current paper.

3.2 Methodological Foundation: Influence Function and Orthogonal Score

In this section, we briefly review the orthogonal score established by Kallus and Mao (2025). Define the nuisance functions

Let 𝜼=(μ~,μ,e,r)\bm{\eta}=(\tilde{\mu},\mu,e,r). Two familiar identification strategies motivate the score. Outcome regression first predicts the observed outcome from (W,X,S)(W,X,S) and then averages that prediction over the surrogate distribution within each arm: τ=𝔼⁡[μ⁡(1,X)−μ⁡(0,X)]\tau=\mathbb{E}[\mu(1,X)-\mu(0,X)]. τ=𝔼⁡[W​R​Ye⁡(X)​r​(1,X,S)−(1−W)​R​Y{1−e⁡(X)}​r​(0,X,S)].\tau=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{WRY}{e(X)r(1,X,S)}-\frac{(1-W)RY}{\{1-e(X)\}r(0,X,S)}\right].

The first strategy can be sensitive to outcome-model error, whereas the second can be unstable when treatment or labeling probabilities are small. The efficient influence function combines them. Specifically, the efficient score is

ψ⁡(Oi,τ,𝜼)\displaystyle\psi(O_{i};\tau,\bm{\eta}) (1)

+Wi​{Ri​(Yi−μ~​(1,Xi,Si))r⁡(1,Xi,Si)+μ~​(1,Xi,Si)−μ⁡(1,Xi)}e⁡(Xi)\displaystyle+\frac{W_{i}\left\{\frac{R_{i}\bigl(Y_{i}-\tilde{\mu}(1,X_{i},S_{i})\bigr)}{r(1,X_{i},S_{i})}+\tilde{\mu}(1,X_{i},S_{i})-\mu(1,X_{i})\right\}}{e(X_{i})}
−(1−Wi)​{Ri​(Yi−μ~​(0,Xi,Si))r⁡(0,Xi,Si)+μ~​(0,Xi,Si)−μ⁡(0,Xi)}1−e⁡(Xi).\displaystyle-\frac{(1-W_{i})\left\{\frac{R_{i}\bigl(Y_{i}-\tilde{\mu}(0,X_{i},S_{i})\bigr)}{r(0,X_{i},S_{i})}+\tilde{\mu}(0,X_{i},S_{i})-\mu(0,X_{i})\right\}}{1-e(X_{i})}.

The first line on the right-hand side is the baseline-adjusted outcome-regression contrast. Within each arm, the term μ~−μ\tilde{\mu}-\mu corrects for how the realized post-treatment surrogate differs from its arm-specific average, and R⁡(Y−μ~)/rR(Y-\tilde{\mu})/r corrects the surrogate prediction using the outcomes that are actually observed. The treatment weights place both corrections on a common experimental population. The function μ⁡(w,x)\mu(w,x) integrates μ~\tilde{\mu} over the arm-ww-specific distribution of the surrogate. This marginalization is essential because Si=Si​(Wi)S_{i}=S_{i}(W_{i}) is post-treatment: the distribution of SiS_{i} observed for treated units (Wi=1)(W_{i}=1) differs from the distribution that would be observed for the same units under control.

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, we have 𝔼⁡[ψ⁡(Oi,τ0,𝜼0)]=0\mathbb{E}[\psi(O_{i};\tau_{0},\bm{\eta}_{0})]=0, where τ0\tau_{0} and 𝜼0\bm{\eta}_{0} denote the true values. Moreover, ψ⁡(O,τ0,𝜼0)\psi(O;\tau_{0},\bm{\eta}_{0}) is the efficient influence function for the ATE in the nonparametric observed-data model under Assumptions 1 and 2, as shown by Kallus and Mao (2025, Theorem 2.1). Consequently, the semiparametric efficiency bound is

V∗=Var⁡{ψ⁡(O,τ0,𝜼0)}=𝔼⁡[ψ​(O,τ0,𝜼0)2].V^{*}=\operatorname{Var}\!\left\{\psi(O;\tau_{0},\bm{\eta}_{0})\right\}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\psi(O;\tau_{0},\bm{\eta}_{0})^{2}\right]. (2)

Thus every regular asymptotically linear estimator has asymptotic variance at least V∗V^{*}, while an estimator with influence function ψ\psi attains this bound. Moreover, Proposition 3 states that the score is robust to certain misspecifications of the nuisance functions, providing conditions under which the estimator remains consistent. In particular, when the treatment propensity is known or consistently estimated, the score is consistent if either the labeling model or the observed-outcome regression is correct in each arm; the marginal regression μ⋆\mu^{\star} need not itself be correct for unbiasedness in that case.

4 SIRNET Details

4.1 Architecture

Figure 1 shows how SIRNET maps the observed data to the nuisance functions required by Equation (1). It is a structured multitask learner for the particular collection of nuisances in that score: a shared adapter lets related prediction tasks inform common embedding directions, while separate heads and input routes enforce the statistical role of each nuisance. The architecture has six blocks.

(i) Baseline encoder. A neural map converts baseline covariates to Bi=bθ​(Xi)B_{i}=b_{\theta}(X_{i}). All downstream nuisance heads use BiB_{i} rather than the raw covariate vector.(ii) Surrogate adapter. A second map adapts a pretrained post-treatment embedding and baseline information to Hi=gθ​(Bi,Si)H_{i}=g_{\theta}(B_{i},S_{i}). When SiS_{i} is represented by a vector of AI scores or pretrained embeddings, gθg_{\theta} is a multilayer adapter that selects and recombines embedding directions for the causal nuisance tasks. (iii) Treatment head. A propensity head estimates e^i=eθ​(Bi)\hat{e}_{i}=e_{\theta}(B_{i}). Under a known randomized design this head can be replaced by the known assignment probability; estimating it can also provide an auxiliary representation-balancing task. (iv) Labeling head. A missingness head estimates r^i​(w)=rθ​(w,Bi,Hi)\hat{r}_{i}(w)=r_{\theta}(w,B_{i},H_{i}), the probability of observing the outcome given treatment, baseline variables, and the surrogate representation. (v) Observed-outcome heads. Two treatment-specific heads estimate μ~^i​(w)=μ~θ​(w,Bi,Hi)\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_{i}(w)=\tilde{\mu}_{\theta}(w,B_{i},H_{i}) for w∈{0,1}w\in\{0,1\}. These heads are trained only on units with Ri=1R_{i}=1 but evaluated for all units in the orthogonal score. (vi) Marginal heads. Two heads estimate μ^i​(w)=μθ​(w,Bi)\hat{\mu}_{i}(w)=\mu_{\theta}(w,B_{i}) for w∈{0,1}w\in\{0,1\}. These heads take only baseline covariates as input, omitting the realized surrogate SiS_{i}, thereby approximating the arm-ww-specific marginal expectation of μ~w\tilde{\mu}_{w} over the distribution of Si​(w)S_{i}(w) given XiX_{i}.

4.2 Training Objective

The network is trained by combining predictive losses for each nuisance function. Let 𝜽\bm{\theta} denote all network parameters. The objective is

ℒ⁡(𝜽)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\bm{\theta})
=λY​1∑iRi​∑i=1nRi​{Yi−μ~^𝜽​(Wi,Bi,Hi)}2\displaystyle=\lambda_{Y}\frac{1}{\sum_{i}R_{i}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}R_{i}\left\{Y_{i}-\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_{\bm{\theta}}(W_{i},B_{i},H_{i})\right\}^{2}
+λR1n∑i=1nℓce(Ri,r^𝜽(Wi,Bi,Hi))+λW1n∑i=1nℓce(Wi,e^𝜽(Bi))\displaystyle+\lambda_{R}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_{\mathrm{ce}}\!\left(R_{i},\hat{r}_{\bm{\theta}}(W_{i},B_{i},H_{i})\right)+\lambda_{W}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_{\mathrm{ce}}\!\left(W_{i},\hat{e}_{\bm{\theta}}(B_{i})\right)
+λM∑w∈{0,1}∑Wi=w{sg⁡(μ~^𝜽​(w,Bi,Hi))−μ^𝜽​(w,Bi)}2∑i𝟏{Wi=w}\displaystyle+\lambda_{M}\sum_{w\in\{0,1\}}\frac{\sum_{W_{i}=w}\left\{\operatorname{sg}\bigl(\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_{\bm{\theta}}(w,B_{i},H_{i})\bigr)-\hat{\mu}_{\bm{\theta}}(w,B_{i})\right\}^{2}}{\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{W_{i}=w\}}

where sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) denotes stop-gradient. The first three terms train the outcome, labeling, and treatment nuisance functions. The fourth term enforces the further marginalization of the outcome heads by matching μθ​(w,Bi)\mu_{\theta}(w,B_{i}) to a stop-gradiented copy of μ~θ​(w,Bi,Hi)\tilde{\mu}_{\theta}(w,B_{i},H_{i}), which prevents this loss from updating the outcome-head-specific parameters through its direct pseudo-outcome, but instead build a joint shared-encoder optimization with a detached pseudo-outcome. This choice follows the broader paradigm of learning from detached, model-generated targets. In representation learning, BYOL (Grill et al., 2020) and SimSiam (Chen and He, 2021) use stop-gradient to prevent direct feedback through prediction targets. Related ideas arise in recursive estimation, including fitted Q-iteration (Ernst et al., 2005) and, more recently, DeepBlip (Ma et al., 2025), which employs detached predictions in recursive neural estimation of causal blip functions. The causal parameter is estimated only after training, by evaluating the cross-fitted orthogonal score.

Moreover, in Appendix A, we introduce additional estimation strategies: regression adjustment and propensity-score weighting, which are complementary to the plug-in orthogonal estimator described above.

Cross-fitting.

In practice, nuisance networks should be estimated with cross-fitting (Chernozhukov et al., 2018): split the data into KK folds, train SIRNET on all but one fold, predict nuisance functions on the held-out fold, and compute the estimator only from out-of-fold predictions (Algorithm 1). Cross-fitting separates nuisance training from score evaluation and allows the use of flexible machine learning while retaining the orthogonal-score interpretation.

4.4 Theoretical Guarantees

The oracle result of Kallus and Mao (2025) gives efficient inference for any cross-fitted nuisances meeting its product-rate conditions. Appendix C gives conditional rates for all seven composite nuisances with a trainable shared encoder, without requiring coordinate recovery. Its supervised-head bound uses one optimization gap for the joint supervised objective, rather than separate empirical optimality for each head. The marginal-head bound additionally requires a final-fit comparison against fixed generated targets over candidate baseline encoders. Neither gap follows from gradient-based training or certifies the fixed architectures used in our experiments.

5 Numerical Validation

5.1 Monte Carlo Validation

In this section, we evaluate the proposed methods on synthetic data to verify the statistical properties.

Data Generating Process

We use two nonlinear DGPs, both with n=1000n=1000 to conduct synthetic experiments. The first uses a construction in which the nuisances have a common nonlinear state along with task-specific components and a protected selection anchor. The second raises the dimensionality and compositional complexity of the nuisance functions and also adds a latent component in the outcome model. The details of the two DGPs can be found in Appendix B.1.

Results on Estimation and Inference

We use 55-fold cross-fitting. The reported methods are complete-case Difference-in-Means; XGBoost regression imputation with XX alone (RI-X) or the realized (X,S)(X,S) (RI-XS); the pooled surrogate-prediction contrast (Pooled-Surr); X-only inverse-probability weighting (IPCW-DiM); the surrogate-only score with XGBoost or SIRNET nuisances; XX-only and full-surrogate Double Machine Learning with XGBoost nuisances; and the full SIRNET score. Appendix B.2 defines these estimators. Every full-score method estimates the treatment propensity. Imputation and surrogate-only intervals use paired-bootstrap refits; full-score intervals use influence-function sandwich standard errors. Table 1 reports bias, empirical SD, RMSE, nominal 95% coverage, and power at the design-specific evaluation point.

Table 1 shows that SIRNET-based estimators provide the strongest overall performance across the two DGPs. In the first DGP, Surr-Only [SIRNET] has the smallest RMSE, reflecting the efficiency gain from the surrogate path when its outcome bridge is well estimated. In the deeper selection-linked DGP, the full SIRNET score has the smallest RMSE among the reported methods, whereas Surr-Only retains big bias. The other methods either have high bias (for example, RI-XS and Pooled-Surr) or high variance (for example, IPCW-DiM and DML-Xonly). These results illustrate both the value of surrogate-informed nuisance learning and the role of the full outcome-residual correction with propensity weighting when the surrogate-only bridge is imperfect.

5.2 Semisynthetic Validation

We complement the fully synthetic experiments with two semisynthetic designs that are calibrated to a real clinical trial. The Anti-Amyloid in Asymptomatic Alzheimer’s Disease (A4) Study (Sperling et al., 2014) was a Phase 3 randomized controlled trial that evaluated solanezumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody targeting soluble amyloid-β\beta, in cognitively unimpaired older adults with elevated cortical amyloid burden on PET imaging. The trial enrolled 1,169 participants (578 assigned to solanezumab and 591 to placebo). Our analysis sample contains 1,129 participants (552 treated and 577 control): it excludes the 40 participants without an eligible post-treatment composite surrogate at either of the two prespecified surrogate visits.

We complement the fully synthetic experiments with two semisynthetic designs that are calibrated to the above real A4 study. In both designs, the n=1129n=1129 observed triples (Xi,Wi,Si)(X_{i},W_{i},S_{i}) are held fixed and only (Yi,Ri)(Y_{i},R_{i}) are redrawn. The baseline input XiX_{i} contains the standardized tabular variables used in the application and the first five principal components of the 1,4881,488-dimensional baseline Swin embedding (Liu et al., 2021). The post-treatment input SiS_{i} contains the first 20 principal components of the 1,489-dimensional composite surrogate embedding.More details on the two semisynthetic designs are provided in Appendix B.7. We use the same estimator grid and five-fold cross-fitting as in Table 1. The SIRNET and fixed-profile strengthened-panel rows use nsim=150n_{\mathrm{sim}}=150 replications at each signal level. The deep-panel classical and XGBoost rows, as well as both fold-local DML-XS reruns, use nsim=300n_{\mathrm{sim}}=300. The results are reported in Table 2.

From Table 2, SIRNET has the smallest RMSE in the strengthened semisynthetic DGP (0.0560.056 versus 0.0670.067 for DML-XS [XGB]), with low bias and near-nominal coverage. SIRNET also has the smallest RMSE in the deep bounded-latent design (0.0560.056), although the jointly fit, fold-local XGBoost pipeline is close (0.0610.061) and likewise has low bias and near-nominal coverage. Thus the A4-calibrated experiments show that both flexible nuisance-learning strategies perform well, with SIRNET retaining a modest RMSE advantage in both designs.

6 Empirical Application: A4 Study

6.1 Study Overview

In this section, we apply the method to the real A4 study. The outcome analyzed here is white matter hyperintensity (WMH) volume, a measure of cerebrovascular burden visible on T2/FLAIR brain MRI. WMH is an established imaging biomarker associated with Alzheimer’s-related neurodegeneration and has been linked to both amyloid pathology and treatment response in preclinical AD populations. We define the analysis outcome as Yi=log⁡(WMHi+1)Y_{i}=\log(\text{WMH}_{i}+1) at month 66, where WMHi\text{WMH}_{i} is WMH volume in mm3. Of the 1129 analysis participants, 797 (70.6%) had an observed month 66 WMH measurement; 332 (29.4%) were missing due to study dropout, death, or missed visits. Among these 332, 11 participants (6 solanezumab, 5 placebo) have a recorded death prior to month 66, accounting for a small share (3.3%3.3\%) of missingness relative to withdrawal (172) and adverse events (51); the remaining reasons are listed in Appendix D.2.

6.2 Features and Surrogate Construction

Baseline covariates (XX). Pre-treatment covariates include tabular clinical and demographic variables (age, sex, years of education, APOE4 allele count, baseline composite amyloid PET score, and baseline cognitive assessment scores) together with a high-dimensional imaging representation derived from the screening visit brain MRI. The screening MRI is encoded by a frozen pretrained Swin Transformer (Liu et al., 2021). Its embedding is compressed to 96 principal components via PCA.

Post-treatment surrogate (SS). We form a composite surrogate from the latest available eligible post-treatment MRI visit: week 84 is preferred and week 12 is used as a fallback. An eligible visit requires both a Swin embedding and a WMH measurement. Of the 1,129 analysis participants, 971 (86.0%) use the week 84 visit and 158 (14.0%) use the week 12 fallback. The raw surrogate contains the 1,4881,488-dimensional frozen embedding and log⁡(WMH+1)\log(\mathrm{WMH}+1) from the assigned visit; it is compressed to 9696 principal components within each training fold, after which SIRNET learns the task-specific surrogate adapter. These post-treatment scans precede the month 66 analysis endpoint and may capture neurological changes related to later dropout and outcome evolution, making conditional MAR more plausible, though it is still not testable.

6.3 Results

We compare the same set of estimators as in the Monte Carlo and semisynthetic experiments, detailed in Appendix B.2. Table 3 shows that the adjusted estimators are broadly consistent with a null effect in the selected analysis cohort. DiM is more negative (τ^=−0.092\hat{\tau}=-0.092), whereas RI-X, the XGBoost DML estimators, and SIRNET are closer to zero and all of their intervals include zero. Thus the selected-cohort analysis provides no evidence of a statistically significant solanezumab effect on month-66 WMH volume. For the full SIRNET row, configuration selection is nested inside each outer training fold: the resulting estimate is −0.044-0.044 (SE 0.0350.035), compared with −0.035-0.035 (SE 0.0350.035) under the earlier globally fixed configuration. Thus the substantive conclusion is insensitive to protecting the outer held-out scores from tuning.

This finding aligns well with the scientific report for the A4 study. The published main results (Sperling et al., 2023) found no statistically significant benefit of solanezumab on PACC or on any secondary cognitive or imaging endpoint. This null finding is consistent with the programme of solanezumab trials in symptomatic patients: both the EXPEDITION 1 and 2 trials in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s disease (Doody et al., 2014) and the subsequent EXPEDITION 3 trial targeting mild dementia (Honig et al., 2018) likewise failed to demonstrate significant slowing of disease progression, suggesting that passive amyloid immunotherapy at the tested doses does not modify the downstream neurodegenerative cascade.

7 Discussion

Summary. SIRNET is a neural implementation of a semiparametric orthogonal moment and a method for causally adapting pretrained surrogate embeddings. It applies a Neyman-orthogonal score that uses actual YY observations to correct the raw surrogate-based estimate, while a shared adapter pools information across the nuisance tasks that determine that score. The empirical claim is consequently about improved nuisance estimation from fixed pretrained embeddings, not about end-to-end representation learning from raw unstructured objects. In the Monte Carlo ablation, this adaptation reduces finite-sample variance and RMSE relative to separately trained neural nuisance networks; a difficulty-matched sharedness continuum (Appendix B.4) further shows the shared representation is at least as accurate as capacity-matched independent networks in both bias and variance across the full range from independent to fully shared nuisances, with no negative-transfer penalty.

Future directions. The most immediate next experiment is to train a pretrained image or text encoder (or a parameter-efficient adapter) inside each cross-fitting fold and compare frozen generic embeddings, outcome-only fine-tuning, independent nuisance adapters, and the shared SIRNET adapter. That experiment would test whether the embedding-level gains documented here extend to end-to-end adaptation of raw unstructured surrogates. Other directions include a sequential neural structure for longitudinal surrogate and outcome data (Shi et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2021; Battocchi et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2025b), conditional average treatment effects, and large-scale multimodal deployments (Kaddour et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2025a; Hu et al., 2026).

Limitations. The conditional MAR assumption requires that all drivers of dropout are captured in (Xi,Si)(X_{i},S_{i}); unmeasured time-varying confounders would invalidate identification. The outcome-only approaches require bootstrap for inference, which is time-consuming for deep-learning based methods. Most importantly for the ML scope, our A4 inputs are frozen pretrained MRI embeddings followed by PCA; the study does not show that SIRNET can learn a useful representation directly from raw images, text, video, or multimodal objects. We leave these extensions to future work.

Appendix

 

Appendix A More on estimation

A.1 Alternative Estimators

Surrogate-only variant. Dropping the R/r⋅(Y−μ~)R/r\cdot(Y-\tilde{\mu}) correction from equation (4.3) yields a surrogate-only score

ψsurr​(Oi,τ,𝜼)\displaystyle\psi^{\mathrm{surr}}(O_{i};\tau,\bm{\eta}) =μ⁡(1,Xi)−μ⁡(0,Xi)−τ\displaystyle=\mu(1,X_{i})-\mu(0,X_{i})-\tau
+Wie⁡(Xi)​[μ~​(1,Xi,Si)−μ⁡(1,Xi)]\displaystyle\quad+\frac{W_{i}}{e(X_{i})}\bigl[\tilde{\mu}(1,X_{i},S_{i})-\mu(1,X_{i})\bigr]
−1−Wi1−e⁡(Xi)​[μ~​(0,Xi,Si)−μ⁡(0,Xi)].\displaystyle\quad-\frac{1-W_{i}}{1-e(X_{i})}\bigl[\tilde{\mu}(0,X_{i},S_{i})-\mu(0,X_{i})\bigr]. (4)

This score omits the observed-outcome residual correction and therefore requires consistent estimation of the outcome regressions μ~\tilde{\mu} and μ\mu (in addition to a correct or known treatment propensity); it is not protected by a correctly specified labeling propensity when those regressions are wrong. Because its influence expression does not account for first-stage outcome-model estimation, the corresponding plug-in standard error can understate sampling variability; paired bootstrap confidence intervals are more reliable for this variant.

Weighting-only variant. Dropping both outcome-regression terms from equation (4.3) yields the inverse-probability-weighted (IPW) score

ψipw​(Oi,τ,e,r)=Wi​Ri​Yie⁡(Xi)​r​(1,Xi,Si)−(1−Wi)​Ri​Yi{1−e⁡(Xi)}​r​(0,Xi,Si)−τ.\displaystyle\psi^{\mathrm{ipw}}(O_{i};\tau,e,r)=\frac{W_{i}R_{i}Y_{i}}{e(X_{i})r(1,X_{i},S_{i})}-\frac{(1-W_{i})R_{i}Y_{i}}{\{1-e(X_{i})\}r(0,X_{i},S_{i})}-\tau. (5)

Its cross-fitted estimator is the sample average of the first two terms in equation (5), using out-of-fold estimates of ee and rr. It does not use μ~\tilde{\mu} or μ\mu, and is consistent when the treatment and labeling propensities are consistently estimated (with ee known under a completely randomized design). Unlike the full score, it has no outcome-regression augmentation and is not Neyman-orthogonal to errors in the estimated propensities. It can consequently be highly variable under weak overlap and sensitive to first-stage propensity error. The usual plug-in influence-function standard error ignores that first-stage contribution unless the propensities are known or estimated sufficiently fast; for the fitted-IPW variant we therefore use paired bootstrap intervals, refitting all nuisance models within each resample. Probability clipping or weight truncation can improve numerical stability in practice.

A.2 Cross-fitting procedure

Algorithm 1 summarizes the cross-fitting procedure for SIRNET.

Appendix B More details on numerical experiments

B.1 Data generating processes

We used the following two DGPs to generate the Monte Carlo results in Tables 1.

B.2 Estimators compared in the Monte Carlo experiments

This subsection defines the method names in Table 1. All machine-learned quantities below are cross-fitted; hats therefore denote out-of-fold predictions. Write ℙn​a=n−1​∑iai\mathbb{P}_{n}a=n^{-1}\sum_{i}a_{i} and nw=∑i𝟏{Wi=w}n_{w}=\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{W_{i}=w\}. For a fitted conditional-outcome model, write m^w(F)=𝔼^[Y∣W=w,R=1,F]\hat{m}_{w}(F)=\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid W=w,R=1,F].

Complete case and imputation baselines.

DiM is the unadjusted complete-case contrast,

τ^DiM=∑iWi​Ri​Yi∑iWi​Ri−∑i(1−Wi)​Ri​Yi∑i(1−Wi)​Ri.\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{DiM}}=\frac{\sum_{i}W_{i}R_{i}Y_{i}}{\sum_{i}W_{i}R_{i}}-\frac{\sum_{i}(1-W_{i})R_{i}Y_{i}}{\sum_{i}(1-W_{i})R_{i}}.

RI-X is ℙn​{m^1​(Xi)−m^0​(Xi)}\mathbb{P}_{n}\{\hat{m}_{1}(X_{i})-\hat{m}_{0}(X_{i})\}, where each outcome model is fitted within treatment arm on observed outcomes. RI-XS uses the same formula with Fi=(Xi,Si)F_{i}=(X_{i},S_{i}). It is deliberately included as a naive benchmark: it evaluates both arm-specific outcome models at the realized post-treatment surrogate Si​(Wi)S_{i}(W_{i}), rather than marginalizing over the surrogate distribution under each arm.

Pooled-Surr fits one pooled model ν^(X,S)≈𝔼[Y∣X,S,R=1]\hat{\nu}(X,S)\approx\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X,S,R=1], ignoring treatment, and contrasts its predictions between the realized treatment groups:

τ^Pooled​-​Surr=1n1​∑iWi​ν^​(Xi,Si)−1n0​∑i(1−Wi)​ν^​(Xi,Si).\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{Pooled\text{-}Surr}}=\frac{1}{n_{1}}\sum_{i}W_{i}\hat{\nu}(X_{i},S_{i})-\frac{1}{n_{0}}\sum_{i}(1-W_{i})\hat{\nu}(X_{i},S_{i}).

Missingness-only and surrogate-only scores.

IPCW-DiM estimates arm-specific X-only labeling models r^w​(X)≈Pr⁡(R=1∣W=w,X)\hat{r}_{w}(X)\approx\Pr(R=1\mid W=w,X) and uses

τ^IPCW=1n1​∑iWi​Ri​Yir^1​(Xi)−1n0​∑i(1−Wi)​Ri​Yir^0​(Xi).\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IPCW}}=\frac{1}{n_{1}}\sum_{i}\frac{W_{i}R_{i}Y_{i}}{\hat{r}_{1}(X_{i})}-\frac{1}{n_{0}}\sum_{i}\frac{(1-W_{i})R_{i}Y_{i}}{\hat{r}_{0}(X_{i})}.

It cannot correct selection that remains associated with SS after conditioning on XX.

For the next two methods, let e^​(X)\hat{e}(X) be the treatment propensity, μ~^w​(X,S)\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_{w}(X,S) the observed-outcome regression, and μ^w​(X)\hat{\mu}_{w}(X) its arm-specific marginalization over SS. Surr-Only uses

ℙn​[μ^1​(Xi)−μ^0​(Xi)+Wie^​(Xi)​{μ~^1​(Xi,Si)−μ^1​(Xi)}−1−Wi1−e^​(Xi)​{μ~^0​(Xi,Si)−μ^0​(Xi)}].\mathbb{P}_{n}\!\left[\hat{\mu}_{1}(X_{i})-\hat{\mu}_{0}(X_{i})+\frac{W_{i}}{\hat{e}(X_{i})}\{\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_{1}(X_{i},S_{i})-\hat{\mu}_{1}(X_{i})\}-\frac{1-W_{i}}{1-\hat{e}(X_{i})}\{\hat{\tilde{\mu}}_{0}(X_{i},S_{i})-\hat{\mu}_{0}(X_{i})\}\right].

It omits the R/rR/r outcome-residual correction. “Surr-Only [XGB]” and “Surr-Only [SIRNET]” differ only in the nuisance learner.

Full orthogonal scores.

DML-Xonly [XGB] uses the ordinary missing-outcome AIPW score with all nuisances conditioned on XX only:

ℙn​[m^1X​(Xi)−m^0X​(Xi)+Wi​Rie^​(Xi)​r^1X​(Xi)​{Yi−m^1X​(Xi)}−(1−Wi)​Ri{1−e^​(Xi)}​r^0X​(Xi)​{Yi−m^0X​(Xi)}].\mathbb{P}_{n}\!\left[\hat{m}^{X}_{1}(X_{i})-\hat{m}^{X}_{0}(X_{i})+\frac{W_{i}R_{i}}{\hat{e}(X_{i})\hat{r}^{X}_{1}(X_{i})}\{Y_{i}-\hat{m}^{X}_{1}(X_{i})\}-\frac{(1-W_{i})R_{i}}{\{1-\hat{e}(X_{i})\}\hat{r}^{X}_{0}(X_{i})}\{Y_{i}-\hat{m}^{X}_{0}(X_{i})\}\right].

DML-XS [XGB] and SIRNET use the full limited-outcome-data orthogonal score in equation (4.3); the former estimates its nuisance functions with XGBoost, while the latter estimates them jointly with SIRNET. Thus DML-XS and SIRNET have the same target score and differ in nuisance estimation, whereas DML-Xonly omits the surrogate from its outcome and labeling nuisances. All estimated probabilities are clipped using the prespecified treatment- and labeling-probability floors before score evaluation.

B.3 Architecture-ablation variants

In this section, we evaluate different architecture-ablation variants of SIRNET to understand the impact of shared and task-specific components on performance. Table 4 holds the observed data, cross-fitting folds, optimizer, loss weights, training budget, early-stopping rule, and probability-clipping rule fixed, and evaluates every variant with the same full orthogonal score. The variants differ only in how nuisance tasks share neural parameters and in the explicitly indicated raw-feature residual paths.

Shared.

This is the default SIRNET. A baseline encoder produces B=bθ​(X)B=b_{\theta}(X) and a surrogate encoder produces H=gθ​(B,S)H=g_{\theta}(B,S). The treatment and marginal heads use BB; the labeling and arm-specific outcome heads use (B,H)(B,H). Thus all nuisance tasks shape the same two encoders.

Partial.

Partial sharing retains the common BB and HH encoders, but gives the outcome and labeling tasks separate residual adapters, HY=H+aY​(H)H_{Y}=H+a_{Y}(H) and HR=H+aR​(H)H_{R}=H+a_{R}(H), before their respective heads. Treatment and marginal heads continue to use BB. This tests whether the outcome and missingness tasks benefit from a small task-private adjustment while preserving the shared representation.

Wide/deep.

Wide/deep retains the shared deep encoders and heads, and adds zero-initialized linear residual paths from the standardized raw inputs: XX for treatment and marginal heads, and (W,X,S)(W,X,S) or (X,S)(X,S) as appropriate for labeling and outcome heads. It therefore tests whether a shallow direct-feature path adds useful task-private capacity beyond the shared nonlinear representation. The residual paths are additive, not replacements for the shared heads.

Partial+wide/deep.

This variant combines the outcome/labeling residual adapters of Partial with the raw-feature linear residual paths of Wide/deep.

Separate.

The Separate baseline has no shared trainable parameters. It fits four independent MLP blocks for e⁡(X)e(X), r⁡(W,X,S)r(W,X,S), μ~​(0,X,S),μ~​(1,X,S)\tilde{\mu}(0,X,S),\tilde{\mu}(1,X,S), and μ⁡(0,X),μ⁡(1,X)\mu(0,X),\mu(1,X), respectively, and then evaluates the same full score. Its marginal block is trained against detached outcome predictions, so it retains the generated-target construction without an encoder-mediated gradient path. It is matched as closely as practical in trainable-parameter count and training budget: 5,426 parameters versus 5,255 for the strengthened-panel shared model, and 20,446 parameters in the deep panel, matched to the wider main-table SIRNET configuration. Consequently, Separate is an ablation of representation sharing, not a different causal estimator.

From Table 4, the shared architecture has the smallest RMSE in the top panel. In the bottom panel, wide/deep is only marginally smaller than shared (0.2610.261 versus 0.2620.262), whereas partial sharing is less precise. This is the anticipated variance–RMSE mechanism: sharing does not make every individual nuisance estimate uniformly less biased, but it can stabilize the collection of nuisances entering the orthogonal score. Overall, the comparison provides direct evidence for the statistical multitask claim, rather than merely showing that a larger neural network works well.

B.4 Ablation on sharedness strength

The main Monte Carlo designs give the nuisance functions both shared and task-specific structure. Here we ask whether sharing network parameters still helps when the response and outcome tasks have less in common. We compare shared SIRNET, a partially shared network, and separate networks while varying the amount of shared signal.

Difficulty-matched design.

Simply weakening a shared signal would also weaken the selection problem. To separate these changes, we use a design indexed by γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1]. The response and outcome tasks each use an index of the form γ​f​(Zcore)+1−γ​f​(Zk)\sqrt{\gamma}\,f(Z_{\mathrm{core}})+\sqrt{1-\gamma}\,f(Z_{k}), where the shared and task-specific terms are independent and have unit variance. Thus each index has the same variance for every γ\gamma: at γ=1\gamma=1 the two tasks use the same latent index, while at γ=0\gamma=0 they use independent indices. The treatment task uses a separate index throughout. A fixed latent factor UU affects the outcome and is visible to the response model only through a noisy, treatment-shifted surrogate coordinate. This maintains selection bias while preserving MAR conditional on (W,X,S)(W,X,S) and the treatment effect τ\tau. Across the grid, complete-case bias stays between −0.13-0.13 and −0.20-0.20, and the outcome SD is about 3.153.15. These diagnostics suggest that the estimation problem remains broadly comparable as sharing varies.

Response calibration.

We keep the true response probability in [0.35,0.90][0.35,0.90]. We also clip estimated response probabilities at 0.250.25, below the true lower bound, to limit the effect of very small predictions.

Results.

Figure 2 reports bias, SD, and RMSE of the full orthogonal score against γ\gamma for the three architectures (n=8000n=8000, nsim=120n_{\mathrm{sim}}=120, K=5K=5 folds; shared 48714871, partial 60236023, and separate 47734773 trainable parameters). Shared and partial networks have lower bias and RMSE than separate networks at every tested γ\gamma, including γ=0\gamma=0. Shared-model bias ranges from −0.010-0.010 to −0.020-0.020 versus −0.029-0.029 to −0.038-0.038 for separate networks; the corresponding RMSE ranges are 0.0730.073–0.0840.084 and 0.0760.076–0.0900.090. Coverage ranges from 0.930.93 to 0.980.98. As a diagnostic, we replace estimated treatment and response probabilities with their true values while retaining the learned outcome heads. The resulting bias is small (+0.004+0.004 to −0.010-0.010) and similar across architectures. A slight increase in bias near γ=1\gamma=1 appears for all methods, including this diagnostic; these results do not isolate its cause.

Interpretation.

In this design, sharing does not incur a large loss even when the response and outcome signals are independent, although it is slighly worse than but almost comparable to separate networks in variance when γ=0\gamma=0. Together with Table 4, the result supports shared nuisance learning for the settings tested here, especially for its ability to maintain a good balance between bias and variance control.

B.5 High-Dimensional Representation-Reuse Diagnostics

In this section we ask a diagnostic question: can a trained shared encoder be handed to a different nuisance learner? We compare raw, shared-SIRNET, and true (oracle) representations in the same five-fold cross-fitted orthogonal score, and compare them with two nuisance learners: Ridge and XGBoost. The results are reported in Table 5. We can see that overall the transfer of the learned representation is beneficial for Ridge but not for XGBoost: XGB/SIRNET has RMSE 0.3840.384 versus 0.3360.336 in the first panel and 0.3900.390 versus 0.3320.332 in the second panel. A paired 30-replication screen with wider (32,32)(32,32) and (32,64)(32,64) embeddings and a deeper, slower XGBoost head gave similar results. The diagnostic therefore supports a narrow conclusion: SIRNET’s encoder can be useful to some replacement heads, but it is not a universally transferable feature map for tree learners.

B.6 Sample-Size Sensitivity

We revisit the two Monte Carlo DGPs with a varying sample size experiment to assess the performance of several strong estimators from Table 1. At each n∈{800,1000,1200,1400,1600,1800}n\in\{800,1000,1200,1400,1600,1800\}, we run nsim=300n_{\mathrm{sim}}=300 independent draws with the DGP functions, network capacity, cross-fitting, and clipping rules held fixed. We retain the two full doubly robust scores (DML-Xonly and DML-XS) together with full SIRNET and Surr-Only [SIRNET], and report bias, empirical SD, and RMSE.

In the first DGP, the two SIRNET scores improve steadily with sample size. Full SIRNET’s RMSE declines from 0.2580.258 at n=800n=800 to 0.1600.160 at n=1800n=1800, while Surr-Only [SIRNET] declines from 0.2040.204 to 0.1360.136 with near-zero bias. Both XGBoost full scores also benefit from larger samples, but remain less precise at n=1800n=1800 (RMSE 0.2130.213 for DML-Xonly and 0.1900.190 for DML-XS).

The deep DGP makes the response correction consequential. Full SIRNET’s RMSE falls from 0.3250.325 to 0.2070.207, below DML-XS (0.4180.418 to 0.2160.216) and DML-Xonly (0.4560.456 to 0.2260.226). Surr-Only [SIRNET] is less variable but retains substantial negative bias, from −0.253-0.253 to −0.203-0.203, whereas full SIRNET reduces it from −0.113-0.113 to −0.055-0.055. Thus larger samples improve nuisance learning, but do not substitute for the full response/outcome correction in the selection-linked mechanism.

Appendix C Theoretical analysis

C.1 Assumptions

In implementation, each SIRNET nuisance head is a feedforward ReLU sub-network attached to a shared encoder output: e^\hat{e} and μ^​(w,⋅)\hat{\mu}(w,\cdot) are functions of Bi=bθ​(Xi)∈ℝdBB_{i}=b_{\theta}(X_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{B}} alone; r^​(w,⋅)\hat{r}(w,\cdot) and μ~^​(w,⋅)\hat{\tilde{\mu}}(w,\cdot) are functions of (Bi,Hi)(B_{i},H_{i}) with Hi=gθ​(Bi,Si)∈ℝdHH_{i}=g_{\theta}(B_{i},S_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{H}}. Writing dgd_{g} for the dimension of the representation feeding head gg (dg=dBd_{g}=d_{B} for e,μe,\mu; dg=dB+dHd_{g}=d_{B}+d_{H} for r,μ~r,\tilde{\mu}), the learned-encoder rate depends on both dgd_{g} and the approximation costs of the encoders. The following assumption describes the component structure used below.

Assumption 3 (Representation sufficiency).

Suppose X∈[−1,1]DXX\in[-1,1]^{D_{X}} and S∈[−1,1]DSS\in[-1,1]^{D_{S}} almost surely. There exist representations Bi0=b0​(Xi)B_{i}^{0}=b_{0}(X_{i}) and Hi0=g0​(Bi0,Si)H_{i}^{0}=g_{0}(B_{i}^{0},S_{i}) of dimensions dB,dHd_{B},d_{H}, and functions e¯0,μ¯0​(w,⋅),r¯0​(w,⋅),μ~¯0​(w,⋅)\bar{e}_{0},\bar{\mu}_{0}(w,\cdot),\bar{r}_{0}(w,\cdot),\bar{\tilde{\mu}}_{0}(w,\cdot) of those representations alone, such that

e0​(Xi)=e¯0​(Bi0),μ0​(w,Xi)=μ¯0​(w,Bi0),r0​(w,Xi,Si)=r¯0​(w,Bi0,Hi0),μ~0​(w,Xi,Si)=μ~¯0​(w,Bi0,Hi0)e_{0}(X_{i})=\bar{e}_{0}(B_{i}^{0}),\quad\mu_{0}(w,X_{i})=\bar{\mu}_{0}(w,B_{i}^{0}),\quad r_{0}(w,X_{i},S_{i})=\bar{r}_{0}(w,B_{i}^{0},H_{i}^{0}),\quad\tilde{\mu}_{0}(w,X_{i},S_{i})=\bar{\tilde{\mu}}_{0}(w,B_{i}^{0},H_{i}^{0})

almost surely, for w=0,1w=0,1. To lighten notation we write e0,μ0,r0,μ~0e_{0},\mu_{0},r_{0},\tilde{\mu}_{0} for e¯0,μ¯0,r¯0,μ~¯0\bar{e}_{0},\bar{\mu}_{0},\bar{r}_{0},\bar{\tilde{\mu}}_{0} from here on, and Bi,HiB_{i},H_{i} for Bi0,Hi0B_{i}^{0},H_{i}^{0}. The coordinates of b0b_{0} and g0g_{0} take values in [−1,1][-1,1] and belong, respectively, to bounded balls in Wpb,∞​([−1,1]DX)W^{p_{b},\infty}([-1,1]^{D_{X}}) and Wph,∞​([−1,1]dB+DS)W^{p_{h},\infty}([-1,1]^{d_{B}+D_{S}}), for fixed integers pb,ph≥1p_{b},p_{h}\geq 1.

Assumption 3 says that the nuisance-relevant information in the high-dimensional inputs has an intrinsic latent-dimensional description. This can be plausible for structured objects such as images and text, whose ambient coordinates are numerous while task-relevant variation may be lower-dimensional. It is nevertheless a substantive approximation assumption, not a consequence of the architecture, the multitask loss, or a pretrained embedding. The theory is developed on this assumption, as is common in deep-network inference analyses (Farrell et al., 2021; Schmidt-Hieber, 2020). To formalize the approximation properties of the nuisance functions on these latent representations, we impose a Sobolev smoothness condition that ensures they can be well-approximated by neural networks.

Assumption 4 (Sobolev smoothness and minimal-rate condition).

For each

g∈{μ~​(1,⋅),μ~​(0,⋅),μ⁡(1,⋅),μ⁡(0,⋅),e,r⁡(1,⋅),r⁡(0,⋅)},g\in\{\tilde{\mu}(1,\cdot),\tilde{\mu}(0,\cdot),\mu(1,\cdot),\mu(0,\cdot),e,r(1,\cdot),r(0,\cdot)\},

the true nuisance g0g_{0} belongs to Wpg,∞​([−1,1]dg)W^{p_{g},\infty}([-1,1]^{d_{g}}), where pgp_{g} is a positive integer. More precisely, writing α=(α1,…,αdg)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d_{g}}) for a multi-index, |α|=∑j=1dgαj|\alpha|=\sum_{j=1}^{d_{g}}\alpha_{j}, and Dα​g0D^{\alpha}g_{0} for the corresponding weak derivative, this means that Dα​g0D^{\alpha}g_{0} exists and is essentially bounded on [−1,1]dg[-1,1]^{d_{g}} for every |α|≤pg|\alpha|\leq p_{g}, with Sobolev norm

‖g0‖Wpg,∞:=max|α|≤pg⁡‖Dα​g0‖L∞​([−1,1]dg)≤K\|g_{0}\|_{W^{p_{g},\infty}}:=\max_{|\alpha|\leq p_{g}}\|D^{\alpha}g_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}([-1,1]^{d_{g}})}\leq K

for a finite constant KK, and

pg>dg/2.p_{g}>d_{g}/2.

Here de=dμ=dBd_{e}=d_{\mu}=d_{B} and dr=dμ~=dB+dHd_{r}=d_{\tilde{\mu}}=d_{B}+d_{H}.

Assumption 4 is imposed on the nuisance functions after their representation coordinates have been rescaled to [−1,1]dg[-1,1]^{d_{g}}; this rescaling is without loss of generality for bounded representations. It says that these functions have uniformly bounded derivatives through order pgp_{g}, thereby ruling out arbitrarily sharp variation in the low-dimensional coordinates. The threshold pg>dg/2p_{g}>d_{g}/2 is exactly the minimal condition for the usual nonparametric exponent to satisfy

pg2​pg+dg>14,\frac{p_{g}}{2p_{g}+d_{g}}>\frac{1}{4},

but the learned-encoder theorem additionally requires pb/DX>1/2p_{b}/D_{X}>1/2 and ph/(dB+DS)>1/2p_{h}/(d_{B}+D_{S})>1/2 to control approximation of the two encoders. These are sufficient smoothness conditions, not a claim that the nuisances are literally Sobolev functions in the original high-dimensional input space. Their burden grows with the ambient encoder-input dimensions as well as the representation dimensions.

C.2 Theoretical Properties

In this section, we discuss the theoretical properties of SIRNET. The first result is a general cross-fitted oracle inference theorem by Kallus and Mao (2025, Theorems 2.1, 3.2, and 3.3), restated in our notation, for the sake of self-containment. It is generally learner-agnostic and applicable on any method that produces cross-fitted nuisance estimators meeting consistency and product-rate conditions. For a cross-fitting fold kk, write PwP_{w} for the distribution conditional on W=wW=w. Define ρe,k=‖e^k−e0‖L2​(P)\rho_{e,k}=\|\hat{e}_{k}-e_{0}\|_{L^{2}(P)} and ρμ⁡(w),k=‖μ^k​(w,⋅)−μ0​(w,⋅)‖L2​(P)\rho_{\mu(w),k}=\|\hat{\mu}_{k}(w,\cdot)-\mu_{0}(w,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}(P)}, where PP is the marginal distribution of XX for these XX-only functions. For g∈{r,μ~}g\in\{r,\tilde{\mu}\}, define ρg⁡(w),k=‖g^k​(w,⋅)−g0​(w,⋅)‖L2​(Pw)\rho_{g(w),k}=\|\hat{g}_{k}(w,\cdot)-g_{0}(w,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}(P_{w})} on (X,S)(X,S). Let ρg\rho_{g} denote the maximum over the fixed number of folds and, where applicable, treatment arms. These arm-specific norms measure errors on the surrogate distribution actually used in each arm’s score, without requiring overlap between the post-treatment surrogate distributions across arms. Equivalently, each arm-specific norm is the L2​(P)L^{2}(P) norm of the corresponding error multiplied by 𝟏{W=w}\mathbf{1}\{W=w\}, divided by Pr⁡(W=w)1/2\Pr(W=w)^{1/2}.

Theorem 1 (Kallus–Mao cross-fitted oracle inference).

Let O1,…,OnO_{1},\ldots,O_{n} be i.i.d., and suppose Assumptions 1 and 2 hold. For a fixed number of cross-fitting folds, suppose each evaluation fold is independent of its nuisance fits. Assume that for both arms

maxw∈{0,1}{ρeρμ⁡(w),ρeρμ~​(w),ρr⁡(w)ρμ~​(w)}=oP(n−1/2),\max_{w\in\{0,1\}}\left\{\rho_{e}\rho_{\mu(w)},\quad\rho_{e}\rho_{\tilde{\mu}(w)},\quad\rho_{r(w)}\rho_{\tilde{\mu}(w)}\right\}=o_{P}(n^{-1/2}), (6)

and the bounded-moment conditions of Kallus and Mao (2025, Assumption 6): for some C<∞C<\infty and q>2q>2, the conditional variances of YY given (W,X,S)(W,X,S) and given (W,X)(W,X), and of μ~0​(W,X,S)\tilde{\mu}_{0}(W,X,S) given (W,X)(W,X), are essentially bounded by CC, while maxw⁡𝔼​|Y⁡(w)|q≤C\max_{w}\mathbb{E}|Y(w)|^{q}\leq C. To apply Theorem 1, we need to ensure that the cross-fitted nuisance estimators satisfy its consistency and product-rate conditions. We now introduce notation for the empirical optimization gaps used in a conditional learned-encoder rate result. For each training fold, let Θn\Theta_{n} be a growing joint ReLU sieve with trainable bθ,gθb_{\theta},g_{\theta}, and let θ^∈Θn\hat{\theta}\in\Theta_{n} be the final fit. These gaps are nonnegative when the fitted outputs belong to their respective classes; defining them does not assert that they are small. In particular, minimizing the full objective (4.2) with its generated marginal target and stop-gradient updates does not guarantee a rate for either gap. Instead, the gaps are a way to state the optimization requirement for the learned-encoder nuisance rates, which is separate from the statistical argument. They also appears in other ways in the literature on deep learning theory, such as in the analyses of deep regression (Schmidt-Hieber, 2020) and empirical minimizers (Farrell et al., 2021). The resulting rate theorem applies to final fits when the order of the optimization gaps shrinks in a certain magnitude as specified in the next theorem. Nevertheless, establishing them for a particular training algorithm is a separate question.

The following theorem gives conditional sufficient rates for the learned-encoder nuisances.

Write 𝒞n=mn​(log⁡n)3\mathcal{C}_{n}=m_{n}(\log n)^{3}.

  • •

    Outcome, propensity, and reponse heads error. For the five directly supervised heads 𝒢sup={e,r⁡(0),r⁡(1),μ~​(0),μ~​(1)}\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{sup}}=\{e,r(0),r(1),\tilde{\mu}(0),\tilde{\mu}(1)\}, the fitted composite nuisances obey

  • •

    Marginalization heads error. For each w∈{0,1}w\in\{0,1\},

Here the gaps and errors denote their maxima across folds. In particular, if δsup,n=oP(n−1/2)\delta_{\mathrm{sup},n}=o_{P}(n^{-1/2}) and maxwδμ⁡(w),n=oP(n−1/2)\max_{w}\delta_{\mu(w),n}=o_{P}(n^{-1/2}), all seven nuisance errors are oP(n−1/4)o_{P}(n^{-1/4}). Under the additional statistical conditions of Theorem 1, its inference conclusions then apply to the learned-encoder score estimator.

Theorem 2 separates approximation, statistical complexity, and the two kinds of optimization gap. The smoothness threshold scomp>1/2s_{\mathrm{comp}}>1/2 constrains both learned encoders and nuisance heads. As long as we train the model to satisfy the optimization conditions, the estimator is asymptotically normal and efficient. Nevertheless, as we have emphasized, the theorem is conditional on the stated gap rates. It does not establish those rates for ordinary gradient-based SIRNET training, which is a separate question.

In particular, a key component that we have adopted in the training process is the stop-gradient operation on the generated targets. Our marginalization objective can be interpreted as a conditional-expectation projection with generated targets. For each treatment arm, the observed-outcome regression supplies detached pseudo-outcomes, which are used to learn their conditional expectation given baseline covariates. This directional dependence is analogous to detached-target recursive learning in DeepBlip (Ma et al., 2025). At the population level, the marginal regression error is bounded by the outcome-regression error plus the marginal projection error. The former is established in the first part of Theorem 2 for the outcome head error term. Our same-fold generated-regressor lemma (Lemma 7) controls the latter under explicit approximation, complexity, and optimization conditions. Stop-gradient prevents direct differentiation through the generated targets, but does not prevent marginalization-loss updates to the shared encoder from affecting subsequent outcome predictions. Accordingly, our theoretical results provide conditional statistical guarantees rather than a convergence guarantee for the joint gradient-based training dynamics.

D.1 A4 study acknowledgement statement

The A4 Study is a secondary prevention trial in preclinical Alzheimer’s disease, aiming to slow cognitive decline associated with brain amyloid accumulation in clinically normal older individuals. The A4 Study is funded by a public-private-philanthropic partnership, including funding from the National Institutes of Health-National Institute on Aging, Eli Lilly and Company, Alzheimer’s Association, Accelerating Medicines Partnership, GHR Foundation, an anonymous foundation and additional private donors, with in-kind support from Avid and Cogstate. The A4 and LEARN Studies are led by Dr. Reisa Sperling at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School and Dr. Paul Aisen at the Alzheimer’s Therapeutic Research Institute (ATRI), University of Southern California. The participants screening for the A4 Study provided permission to share their de-identified data in order to advance the quest to find a successful treatment for Alzheimer’s disease. D.2 A4 Overlap and Missingness Sensitivity Diagnostics

The conditional MAR assumption cannot be tested from the observed data. We therefore report diagnostics that check its empirical implications and the stability of the weighting correction.

Missingness reasons and death.

Table 6 breaks down the 332 participants with missing month 66 WMH by their recorded reason for study discontinuation. Subject withdrawal (172) and adverse events (51) account for most of the missingness; 11 participants (6 solanezumab, 5 placebo) have a recorded death before month 66. Because Yi​(w)=log⁡(WMHi​(w)+1)Y_{i}(w)=\log(\mathrm{WMH}_{i}(w)+1) is not well defined for a participant who dies before the month 66 visit under arm ww, treating these 11 cases as ordinary missing-at-random nonresponse is less appropriate. Nevertheless, with only 11 of 1129 participants (1.0%) affected, this choice is unlikely to materially change the point estimate, but we flag it explicitly rather than leave death implicitly folded into “dropout.”

The diagnostic refit uses one five-fold cross-fit of the selected architecture and the n=1129n=1129 analysis sample. Outcome observation rates are nearly equal in the control and treatment arms (70.5% and 70.7%, respectively). As shown in Figure 5, the estimated treatment propensity has broad support (1st–99th percentile: 0.175–0.841). The observed-arm labeling propensity has a median of 0.740, although its minimum is 0.012. Consequently, the observed-case weights have a long right tail: the 99th percentile is 15.0 and the maximum is 104.0. Therefore, we adopted proper trimming in the implementation to mitigate the outlier weights and keep the estimator stable. Table 7 shows that, over labeling-propensity floors from 0.05 to 0.15, the point estimate ranges from −0.013-0.013 to −0.008-0.008 and every interval includes zero. Lowering the floor to 0.01 increases the standard error and moves the point estimate to −0.001-0.001, illustrating the influence of the extreme tail without changing the qualitative conclusion.

Appendix E Computational aspects

Time.

Let nn be the number of observations, PP the number of trainable SIRNET parameters, EE the epochs actually run (bounded by the configured maximum), and KK the number of cross-fitting folds. For the dense feedforward network, one forward/backward pass costs O⁡(P)O(P) per observation, up to the fixed number of nuisance heads. Adam training on one fold therefore costs O⁡(E​n​P)O(EnP) in the worst case; held-out prediction and score aggregation cost O⁡(n​P)O(nP) and O⁡(n)O(n), respectively. A standard KK-fold round fits KK networks on approximately n⁡(K−1)/Kn(K-1)/K observations each, giving O⁡(E⁡(K−1)​n​P)O(E(K-1)nP) training time, plus fold-local preprocessing. Repeating the round RR times multiplies this cost by RR. For nested tuning with CC candidate configurations and JJ inner folds, each outer fold fits C​JCJ inner models and refits one selected model. The implementation thus trains R​K​(C​J+1)RK(CJ+1) networks; for the A4 full-score analysis, R=5R=5, K=5K=5, C=3C=3, and J=2J=2 give 175 fits. These counts are an upper-bound guide to workload, not measured wall-clock times: early stopping, candidate widths, PCA, and hardware affect actual runtime. Each split fits its scalers and, for A4, the baseline and surrogate PCA maps on training data only.

Space and sample size.

The fitted network and Adam’s parameter and moment arrays require O⁡(P)O(P) storage, while minibatch activations scale with batch size and layer widths. Holding the preprocessed sample and out-of-fold scores requires space linear in nn and the input dimensions; the A4 pipeline also holds the raw imaging embeddings and PCA work arrays during preprocessing. Models are fitted one split at a time rather than keeping all R​K​(C​J+1)RK(CJ+1) models in memory. An outer fit uses approximately n⁡(K−1)/Kn(K-1)/K units before its early-stopping split; an inner candidate fit uses approximately n⁡(K−1)​(J−1)/(K​J)n(K-1)(J-1)/(KJ) units before that split. With n=1129n=1129, K=5K=5, J=2J=2, and a 15% validation fraction, these are roughly 770 and 380 training units, respectively. Outcome-head training uses only observed outcomes in the relevant treatment arm, so its effective sample is smaller still (the A4 outcome is observed for 797 of 1129 analysis participants).

Computing infrastructure.

The experiment server documented for this project has one NVIDIA H100 GPU with 80 GB of memory. Its workspace allocation is limited to approximately 14 CPU cores and 146 GiB of RAM. The neural simulation launch scripts request CUDA for SIRNET fits, whereas classical and XGBoost baseline jobs use bounded CPU parallelism. A4 SIRNET runs also request CUDA; the training code falls back to CPU if a GPU is unavailable. GPU access depends on the execution environment: the managed sandbox does not expose the host GPU, so a CUDA job must run in a GPU-enabled allocation. The recorded configuration describes the project server, not a per-run hardware log or a measured runtime for each reported experiment.

Appendix F Hyperparameter Tuning

F.1 SIRNET

SIRNET has architecture parameters that control the shared baseline and surrogate embeddings, and loss weights (λY,λR,λW,λM)(\lambda_{Y},\lambda_{R},\lambda_{W},\lambda_{M}) that balance the four jointly trained heads.

Nested tuning for the full score.

The full-score A4 analysis uses nested tuning rather than a global validation screen. For each outer K=5K=5 training partition, we evaluate the three fixed candidate configurations in Table 8 by two-fold inner cross-fitting. The inner criterion is the standard deviation of the out-of-fold per-unit orthogonal scores. We then refit the selected configuration on the full outer training partition (with a training-only early-stopping split) and evaluate it only on the untouched outer fold. Thus a participant’s outcome and influence contribution cannot affect the configuration used for that participant’s final score. The procedure is repeated for five outer K=5K=5 rounds. Early stopping uses at most 300 epochs with patience 40, and all configurations use the response-probability score floor rclip=0.05r_{\mathrm{clip}}=0.05.

The compact regularized candidate is selected in 22 of the 25 outer folds; the balanced and outcome-bridge candidates are selected in 2 and 1 folds, respectively. The surrogate-only analysis remains a separately reported bootstrap-based descriptive estimator and does not supply the full-score orthogonal-inference result.

Final seed averaging and inference.

To reduce variance from randomness in neural network training, we employ a five-seed averaging strategy. For full SIRNET, we average the out-of-fold influence values over five independently seeded, nested K=5K=5 cross-fitting rounds before computing the ATE and its influence-function SE. For Surr-Only [SIRNET], which uses bootstrap inference, the point estimate is the mean of five independently initialized shared-network fits. Each of the B=200B=200 paired bootstrap draws repeats the same five-seed averaging, so its bootstrap SE incorporates both sampling variation and the observed optimization sensitivity.

F.2 Baseline nuisance estimators and XGBoost selection

Ridge baselines use fixed configurations. For the direct DML-XS–SIRNET comparisons in Tables 1 and 2, however, we tune the full XGBoost nuisance pipeline with the same split discipline as the causal estimator: profile selection occurs inside each outer training partition, and the selected pipeline is refit before scoring the untouched outer fold.

Ridge (linear nuisances).

Outcome models μw​(X)\mu_{w}(X) and μ~w​(X,S)\tilde{\mu}_{w}(X,S) use sklearn Ridge(α=1.0\alpha=1.0) with zz-scored inputs. Selection models rw​(X)r_{w}(X) and rw​(X,S)r_{w}(X,S) use LogisticRegression with ℓ2\ell_{2} penalty (C=1.0C=1.0) and standardised inputs.

XGBoost.

For the nested DML-XS rows, each candidate specifies the complete nuisance pipeline: treatment and labeling classifiers, observed-outcome regressions, and the generated marginal regressions all use the same profile. In every outer fold, we compare the three profiles in Table 9 by the standard deviation of their inner out-of-fold orthogonal scores, then refit the winner on the outer training data.

Bootstrap standard errors.

Imputation-only methods (RI-X, RI-XS, pooled surrogate-prediction contrast, Surr-Only) use B=30B=30 bootstrap resamples for variance estimation in the MC and semisynthetic experiments, and B=200B=200 in the A4 empirical application. The simulation choice is computational: every bootstrap draw refits the full KK-fold nuisance pipeline, nested inside 300 Monte Carlo replications, two signal levels, two DGPs, and two learner families. The point estimates, empirical SD, and RMSE do not depend on BB; only the replicate-specific bootstrap interval does.

μ0​w(X)=𝔼{μ~0(w,X,S)∣W=w,X}.\mu_{0w}(X)=\mathbb{E}\{\tilde{\mu}_{0}(w,X,S)\mid W=w,X\}.
