{e⋆=e0orμ⋆(w,⋅)=μ0​w}and{r⋆(w,⋅)=r0(w,⋅)orμ~⋆(w,⋅)=μ~0(w,⋅)}.\{e^{\star}=e_{0}\ \text{or}\ \mu^{\star}(w,\cdot)=\mu_{0w}\}\quad\text{and}\quad\{r^{\star}(w,\cdot)=r_{0}(w,\cdot)\ \text{or}\ \tilde{\mu}^{\star}(w,\cdot)=\tilde{\mu}_{0}(w,\cdot)\}.

Proposition 3 shows that the efficient score is robust to certain types of nuisance function misspecifications. In particular, it remains consistent as long as either the propensity score or the outcome regression is correctly specified for each treatment arm, and either the missingness mechanism or the imputed outcome is correctly specified for each arm.

G.2 Collection of technical lemmas and proofs

Approximation and complexity for the learned joint sieve.

Yarotsky’s approximation result (Lemma 4) explains the Sobolev exponent; the bounded-weight construction of Schmidt-Hieber (2020, Theorem 5) supplies approximants for the actual sieve. Lemma 5 controls complexity, and Lemma 6 supplies the direct-head risk bound.

Lemma 4 (ReLU approximation of Sobolev balls; Yarotsky, 2017, Theorem 1).

Fix d≥1d\geq 1, integer p≥1p\geq 1, and 0<K<∞0<K<\infty. There is a constant Cd,p,K<∞C_{d,p,K}<\infty such that for every f0∈Wp,∞​([−1,1]d)f_{0}\in W^{p,\infty}([-1,1]^{d}) with ‖f0‖Wp,∞≤K\|f_{0}\|_{W^{p,\infty}}\leq K and every ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), there exists a feedforward ReLU network ff with depth at most Cd,p,K​(log⁡(1/ϵ)+1)C_{d,p,K}(\log(1/\epsilon)+1) and at most Cd,p,Kϵ−d/p(log(1/ϵ)+1)C_{d,p,K}\epsilon^{-d/p}(\log(1/\epsilon)+1) weights and computation units, such that supx∈[−1,1]d|f⁡(x)−f0​(x)|≤ϵ\sup_{x\in[-1,1]^{d}}|f(x)-f_{0}(x)|\leq\epsilon.

Lemma 4 is a statement purely about what a ReLU network can represent; it involves no data, no randomness, and no estimation. To account for the statistical error of estimating a function from data, we need to bound the covering number of the class of networks of a given size. The following lemma gives a covering-number bound for a class of ReLU networks with bounded depth, width, and parameter magnitude.

For the bounded-weight sieve used below we use the constructive approximation bound of Schmidt-Hieber (2020, Theorem 5), rather than infer a weight bound from Lemma 4. Applied to both trainable encoders and all seven heads on their respective bounded input domains, it yields the joint composite approximation and entropy bounds in the proof of Theorem 2.

Lemma 5 (Covering number of a ReLU network class).

For integers L,W≥1L,W\geq 1 and B≥1B\geq 1, let ℱ⁡(L,W,B)\mathcal{F}(L,W,B) denote the functions [−1,1]d→ℝ[-1,1]^{d}\to\mathbb{R} computed by a feedforward ReLU network of a fixed architecture with LL hidden layers and WW total (weight and bias) parameters, each parameter ranging over [−B,B][-B,B]. Then for every δ∈(0,1]\delta\in(0,1],

log𝒩(δ,ℱ(L,W,B),∥⋅∥∞)≤W(L+4)log(B(W+1))+Wlog(4B/δ).\log\mathcal{N}\bigl(\delta,\mathcal{F}(L,W,B),\|\cdot\|_{\infty}\bigr)\;\leq\;W(L+4)\log\bigl(B(W+1)\bigr)+W\log(4B/\delta).

If ℱs​(L,W,B)\mathcal{F}_{s}(L,W,B) restricts this architecture to at most s∈{1,…,W}s\in\{1,\ldots,W\} nonzero parameters, then

log𝒩(δ,ℱs(L,W,B),∥⋅∥∞)≤slog(eW/s)+s(L+4)log(B(W+1))+slog(4B/δ).\log\mathcal{N}\bigl(\delta,\mathcal{F}_{s}(L,W,B),\|\cdot\|_{\infty}\bigr)\leq s\log(eW/s)+s(L+4)\log\bigl(B(W+1)\bigr)+s\log(4B/\delta).
Proof.

Write fθf_{\theta} for the network with parameter vector θ∈[−B,B]W\theta\in[-B,B]^{W}, with layer activations aθ(0)​(x)=xa_{\theta}^{(0)}(x)=x, aθ(ℓ)​(x)=ReLU⁡(Wθ(ℓ)​aθ(ℓ−1)​(x)+bθ(ℓ))a_{\theta}^{(\ell)}(x)=\mathrm{ReLU}\bigl(W^{(\ell)}_{\theta}a_{\theta}^{(\ell-1)}(x)+b^{(\ell)}_{\theta}\bigr) for ℓ=1,…,L\ell=1,\ldots,L, and fθ​(x)=Wθ(L+1)​aθ(L)​(x)+bθ(L+1)f_{\theta}(x)=W^{(L+1)}_{\theta}a_{\theta}^{(L)}(x)+b^{(L+1)}_{\theta}. Let Γ:=B⁡(W+1)≥2\Gamma:=B(W+1)\geq 2.

Layer bound. We show ‖aθ(ℓ)​(x)‖∞≤Γℓ+1\|a_{\theta}^{(\ell)}(x)\|_{\infty}\leq\Gamma^{\ell+1} for all ℓ=0,…,L\ell=0,\ldots,L and x∈[−1,1]dx\in[-1,1]^{d}, by induction. The base case ℓ=0\ell=0 holds since ‖x‖∞≤1≤Γ\|x\|_{\infty}\leq 1\leq\Gamma. For the step, since the network has at most WW total parameters, each unit has at most WW incoming weights, so each coordinate of the pre-activation z(ℓ)=Wθ(ℓ)​aθ(ℓ−1)​(x)+bθ(ℓ)z^{(\ell)}=W^{(\ell)}_{\theta}a_{\theta}^{(\ell-1)}(x)+b^{(\ell)}_{\theta} satisfies |zk(ℓ)|≤B​W​‖aθ(ℓ−1)​(x)‖∞+B≤B​W​Γℓ+B​Γℓ=Γℓ+1|z^{(\ell)}_{k}|\leq BW\|a_{\theta}^{(\ell-1)}(x)\|_{\infty}+B\leq BW\Gamma^{\ell}+B\Gamma^{\ell}=\Gamma^{\ell+1} (using the inductive hypothesis and Γℓ≥1\Gamma^{\ell}\geq 1). Since |ReLU⁡(t)|≤|t||\mathrm{ReLU}(t)|\leq|t|, ‖aθ(ℓ)​(x)‖∞≤Γℓ+1\|a_{\theta}^{(\ell)}(x)\|_{\infty}\leq\Gamma^{\ell+1}, completing the induction; the same bound gives |fθ​(x)|≤ΓL+2|f_{\theta}(x)|\leq\Gamma^{L+2}.

Lipschitz bound. Fix θ,θ′∈[−B,B]W\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in[-B,B]^{W} with η:=‖θ−θ′‖∞\eta:=\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{\infty}, and let ηℓ:=supx‖aθ(ℓ)​(x)−aθ′(ℓ)​(x)‖∞\eta_{\ell}:=\sup_{x}\|a_{\theta}^{(\ell)}(x)-a_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(\ell)}(x)\|_{\infty}, so η0=0\eta_{0}=0. As above, each coordinate of z(ℓ)−z′(ℓ)z^{(\ell)}-z^{\prime(\ell)} is a sum of at most WW weight-difference terms, a weight-times-activation-difference term, and a bias-difference term, so

|zk(ℓ)−zk′(ℓ)|≤B​W​ηℓ−1+W​η​Γℓ+η≤Γ​ηℓ−1+Γℓ+1​η,|z^{(\ell)}_{k}-z^{\prime(\ell)}_{k}|\;\leq\;BW\eta_{\ell-1}+W\eta\,\Gamma^{\ell}+\eta\;\leq\;\Gamma\,\eta_{\ell-1}+\Gamma^{\ell+1}\eta,

using ‖aθ′(ℓ−1)​(x)‖∞≤Γℓ\|a_{\theta^{\prime}}^{(\ell-1)}(x)\|_{\infty}\leq\Gamma^{\ell} from the layer bound applied to θ′\theta^{\prime}, B​W≤ΓBW\leq\Gamma, and W​Γℓ+1≤(W+1)​Γℓ≤Γℓ+1W\Gamma^{\ell}+1\leq(W+1)\Gamma^{\ell}\leq\Gamma^{\ell+1}. Since ReLU is 11-Lipschitz, ηℓ≤Γ​ηℓ−1+Γℓ+1​η\eta_{\ell}\leq\Gamma\eta_{\ell-1}+\Gamma^{\ell+1}\eta, and by induction on ℓ\ell (base case η0=0\eta_{0}=0), ηℓ≤ℓ​Γℓ+1​η\eta_{\ell}\leq\ell\,\Gamma^{\ell+1}\eta. Applying the same one-step bound to the (linear) output layer,

‖fθ−fθ′‖∞≤Γ​ηL+ΓL+2​η≤Γ⋅L​ΓL+1​η+ΓL+2​η≤(L+1)​ΓL+2​η≤ΓL+4​η,\|f_{\theta}-f_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{\infty}\;\leq\;\Gamma\,\eta_{L}+\Gamma^{L+2}\eta\;\leq\;\Gamma\cdot L\Gamma^{L+1}\eta+\Gamma^{L+2}\eta\;\leq\;(L+1)\Gamma^{L+2}\eta\;\leq\;\Gamma^{L+4}\eta,

using L≤W≤ΓL\leq W\leq\Gamma in the last step.

Covering argument. By the Lipschitz bound, an η\eta-net of the parameter box [−B,B]W[-B,B]^{W} in ∥⋅∥∞\|\cdot\|_{\infty}, with η=δ/ΓL+4\eta=\delta/\Gamma^{L+4}, induces a δ\delta-net of ℱ⁡(L,W,B)\mathcal{F}(L,W,B) in sup norm over x∈[−1,1]dx\in[-1,1]^{d}. A standard grid construction gives such an η\eta-net of [−B,B]W[-B,B]^{W} of size at most (4​B/η)W(4B/\eta)^{W} (for η≤B\eta\leq B), so

𝒩(δ,ℱ(L,W,B),∥⋅∥∞)≤(4​B​ΓL+4δ)W,\mathcal{N}(\delta,\mathcal{F}(L,W,B),\|\cdot\|_{\infty})\;\leq\;\Bigl(\frac{4B\Gamma^{L+4}}{\delta}\Bigr)^{W},

and taking logarithms and substituting Γ=B⁡(W+1)\Gamma=B(W+1) gives the first bound. For the sparse class, fix a support of size at most ss. The same Lipschitz constant applies, while a parameter grid on that support needs at most (4​B​ΓL+4/δ)s(4B\Gamma^{L+4}/\delta)^{s} points. There are at most ∑j=0s(Wj)≤(e​W/s)s\sum_{j=0}^{s}\binom{W}{j}\leq(eW/s)^{s} such supports. Taking the union of their grids and then logarithms gives the second bound. A fixed coordinatewise clipping of the outputs does not enlarge either covering number. ∎

Lemma 6 (Least-squares oracle inequality for approximate ERM).

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} consist of functions [−1,1]d→[−M,M][-1,1]^{d}\to[-M,M], where M≥1M\geq 1, and suppose log𝒩(δ,ℱ,∥⋅∥∞)≤Alog(A0/δ)\log\mathcal{N}(\delta,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})\leq A\log(A_{0}/\delta) for 0<δ≤M0<\delta\leq M, with A≥1A\geq 1 and A0≥max⁡{e,M}A_{0}\geq\max\{e,M\}. Let (xi,Yi)i=1n(x_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1}^{n} be i.i.d., Yi=f0​(xi)+ϵiY_{i}=f_{0}(x_{i})+\epsilon_{i}, ‖f0‖∞≤M\|f_{0}\|_{\infty}\leq M, and suppose 𝔼⁡[ϵi∣xi]=0\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{i}\mid x_{i}]=0 and the errors are uniformly conditionally sub-Gaussian with parameter σ\sigma. Suppose f^∈ℱ\hat{f}\in\mathcal{F} satisfies

Pn​(Y−f^)2≤inff∈ℱPn​(Y−f)2+δnP_{n}(Y-\hat{f})^{2}\leq\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}}P_{n}(Y-f)^{2}+\delta_{n}

for a nonnegative, possibly data-dependent δn\delta_{n}. For n≥2n\geq 2, there is a universal constant CC such that, if 𝔼​δn<∞\mathbb{E}\delta_{n}<\infty,

𝔼​‖f^−f0‖L2​(P)2≤C​inff∈ℱ‖f−f0‖∞2+C⁡(M2+σ2)​A​log⁡(A0​n)n+C​𝔼​δn.\mathbb{E}\|\hat{f}-f_{0}\|_{L^{2}(P)}^{2}\leq C\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\|f-f_{0}\|_{\infty}^{2}+C(M^{2}+\sigma^{2})\frac{A\log(A_{0}n)}{n}+C\mathbb{E}\delta_{n}.

This is the localized least-squares oracle-inequality argument adapted to conditional sub-Gaussian errors; it is not a direct restatement of the Gaussian-noise result of Schmidt-Hieber (2020, Lemma 4) (see also Györfi et al., 2002, Ch. 11). The corresponding high-probability approximate-ERM bound has δn\delta_{n} in place of 𝔼​δn\mathbb{E}\delta_{n} and yields the OPO_{P} rate used in the theorem without an expectation assumption on δn\delta_{n}. A fixed pointwise clipping map is 11-Lipschitz and therefore cannot increase a class’s sup-norm covering number. It does not increase approximation error only if the target lies inside the clipping interval. Outcome predictions are clipped to [−M,M][-M,M]; the clipping thresholds for ee and rr are chosen within their respective true overlap bounds.

For Bernoulli cross-entropy, let p0​(v)=Pr⁡(Y=1∣V=v)p_{0}(v)=\Pr(Y=1\mid V=v) and suppose both p0​(v)p_{0}(v) and p⁡(v)p(v) lie in [ϵ,1−ϵ][\epsilon,1-\epsilon]. Then

𝔼{ℓce(Y,p(V))−ℓce(Y,p0(V))}=𝔼[KL{Bern(p0(V))∥Bern(p(V))}]≥2∥p−p0∥L2​(P)2,\mathbb{E}\{\ell_{\rm ce}(Y,p(V))-\ell_{\rm ce}(Y,p_{0}(V))\}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\operatorname{KL}\{\operatorname{Bern}(p_{0}(V))\|\operatorname{Bern}(p(V))\}\right]\geq 2\|p-p_{0}\|_{L^{2}(P)}^{2},

where the inequality is Pinsker’s inequality. Pinsker alone does not establish an estimation rate. On this clipping interval, cross-entropy losses are bounded and Lipschitz, and their excess losses satisfy a Bernstein condition. Localizing their entropy bound gives, for an approximate empirical minimizer over a class 𝒫\mathcal{P} with the entropy bound of Lemma 6,

‖p^−p0‖L2​(P)2=OP​(infp∈𝒫‖p−p0‖∞2+A​log⁡(A0​n)n+δn),\|\hat{p}-p_{0}\|_{L^{2}(P)}^{2}=O_{P}\!\left(\inf_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\|p-p_{0}\|_{\infty}^{2}+\frac{A\log(A_{0}n)}{n}+\delta_{n}\right),

with constants depending on ϵ\epsilon. The sup-norm approximation term is quadratic because the Bernoulli KL divergence has bounded curvature on this interval.

The five directly supervised heads fit observed labels: ee uses WW, r⁡(w)r(w) uses RR in arm ww, and μ~​(w)\tilde{\mu}(w) uses YY among labeled units in arm ww. The marginal target μ0​(w,X)\mu_{0}(w,X) is never observed. Its fit instead uses predictions from the final outcome head on the same training fold and with a learned baseline encoder. The next lemma controls this generated-regressor step in terms of the empirical gap δμ⁡(w),n\delta_{\mu(w),n} defined in (8).

The Marginal Head: A Generated-Regressor Lemma.

The marginal head μ^​(w,⋅)\hat{\mu}(w,\cdot) targets μ0(w,x)=𝔼[μ~0(w,X,S)∣W=w,X=x]\mu_{0}(w,x)=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mu}_{0}(w,X,S)\mid W{=}w,X{=}x], which is itself a functional of μ~0\tilde{\mu}_{0}: fitting μ^​(w,⋅)\hat{\mu}(w,\cdot) is a generated-regressor problem, with pseudo-outcome μ~^​(w,Xi,Si)\hat{\tilde{\mu}}(w,X_{i},S_{i}) rather than the true μ~0​(w,Xi,Si)\tilde{\mu}_{0}(w,X_{i},S_{i}). The training loss (4.2) stop-gradients this pseudo-outcome, but the two heads still use the same training-fold observations. The uniform bound below handles their dependence over learned-encoder composite classes.

Lemma 7 (Learned-encoder same-fold marginal rate).

Fix w∈{0,1}w\in\{0,1\} and write 𝒬m,w\mathcal{Q}_{m,w} for the bounded, clipped composite outcome class (x,s)↦qw​(b⁡(x),g⁡(b⁡(x),s))(x,s)\mapsto q_{w}(b(x),g(b(x),s)); let ℱm,w\mathcal{F}_{m,w} be the composite marginal class defined before Theorem 2. The jointly fitted q^\hat{q} and f^\hat{f} belong to these classes. Let PwP_{w} denote expectation given W=wW=w. Suppose their sup-norm covering numbers satisfy Tn:=logn+log𝒩(1/n,𝒬m,w,∥⋅∥∞)+log𝒩(1/n,ℱm,w,∥⋅∥∞)T_{n}:=\log n+\log\mathcal{N}(1/n,\mathcal{Q}_{m,w},\|\cdot\|_{\infty})+\log\mathcal{N}(1/n,\mathcal{F}_{m,w},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}). For the gap δμ⁡(w),n\delta_{\mu(w),n} in (8),

ρμ⁡(w,⋅)2=OP​(inff∈ℱm,w‖f−μ0​(w,⋅)‖∞2+Tnn+δμ⁡(w),n+ρμ~​(w,⋅)2).\rho_{\mu(w,\cdot)}^{2}=O_{P}\!\left(\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{m,w}}\|f-\mu_{0}(w,\cdot)\|_{\infty}^{2}+\frac{T_{n}}{n}+\delta_{\mu(w),n}+\rho_{\tilde{\mu}(w,\cdot)}^{2}\right). (10)
Proof.

Write q0=μ~0​(w,⋅)q_{0}=\tilde{\mu}_{0}(w,\cdot) and q0​(X,S)=μ0​(w,X)+ξq_{0}(X,S)=\mu_{0}(w,X)+\xi, where 𝔼[ξ∣W=w,X]=0\mathbb{E}[\xi\mid W=w,X]=0. Choose a deterministic comparator f∗∈ℱm,wf^{*}\in\mathcal{F}_{m,w} and set a=‖f∗−μ0​(w,⋅)‖L2​(Pw)a=\|f^{*}-\mu_{0}(w,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}(P_{w})}. For q∈𝒬m,wq\in\mathcal{Q}_{m,w} and f∈ℱm,wf\in\mathcal{F}_{m,w}, set

Dq,f:=(q−f)2−(q−f∗)2.D_{q,f}:=(q-f)^{2}-(q-f^{*})^{2}.

Because all functions are clipped, Dq,fD_{q,f} is bounded and Varw⁡(Dq,f)≤C​Pw​(f−f∗)2\operatorname{Var}_{w}(D_{q,f})\leq C\,P_{w}(f-f^{*})^{2}. A product cover of 𝒬m,w×ℱm,w\mathcal{Q}_{m,w}\times\mathcal{F}_{m,w} at sup-norm resolution 1/n1/n has log cardinality at most TnT_{n}. For a fixed element of that cover, Bernstein’s inequality with a union bound over the cover gives, simultaneously and with probability tending to one,

|(Pw−Pn,w)​Dq,f|≤C​Pw​(f−f∗)2​Tn/n+C​Tn/n.|(P_{w}-P_{n,w})D_{q,f}|\leq C\sqrt{P_{w}(f-f^{*})^{2}\,T_{n}/n}+CT_{n}/n.

Here nw≍nn_{w}\asymp n by treatment overlap. The squared-loss difference is Lipschitz in (q,f)(q,f) on the clipped range, so passing from the cover to the full class adds O⁡(1/n)O(1/n). Applying Young’s inequality to the square-root term gives

|(Pw−Pn,w)​Dq,f|≤18​Pw​(f−f∗)2+C​Tnn\left|(P_{w}-P_{n,w})D_{q,f}\right|\leq\tfrac{1}{8}P_{w}(f-f^{*})^{2}+C\frac{T_{n}}{n} (11)

simultaneously for all q,fq,f, with probability tending to one. This step is uniform over the composite classes, so it applies to q^\hat{q} and f^\hat{f} even when their encoders were fitted on these observations.

Apply (11) and (8) with q=q^,f=f^q=\hat{q},f=\hat{f}. Put e=q^−q0e=\hat{q}-q_{0}. Since 𝔼[ξ∣W=w,X]=0\mathbb{E}[\xi\mid W=w,X]=0,

Pw​{(q^−f^)2−(q^−f∗)2}=Pw​(f^−μ0)2−a2+2​Pw​{e⁡(f∗−f^)}≥34​Pw​(f^−μ0)2−C​a2−C​‖e‖L2​(Pw)2,P_{w}\{(\hat{q}-\hat{f})^{2}-(\hat{q}-f^{*})^{2}\}=P_{w}(\hat{f}-\mu_{0})^{2}-a^{2}+2P_{w}\{e(f^{*}-\hat{f})\}\geq\tfrac{3}{4}P_{w}(\hat{f}-\mu_{0})^{2}-Ca^{2}-C\|e\|_{L^{2}(P_{w})}^{2},

where Cauchy–Schwarz and Young’s inequality bound the term involving ee. Also Pw​(f^−f∗)2≤2​Pw​(f^−μ0)2+2​a2P_{w}(\hat{f}-f^{*})^{2}\leq 2P_{w}(\hat{f}-\mu_{0})^{2}+2a^{2}. Combining these bounds with the empirical excess risk and absorbing the 18​Pw​(f^−f∗)2\tfrac{1}{8}P_{w}(\hat{f}-f^{*})^{2} term yields Pw​(f^−μ0)2=OP​(a2+Tn/n+δμ⁡(w),n+‖e‖L2​(Pw)2)P_{w}(\hat{f}-\mu_{0})^{2}=O_{P}(a^{2}+T_{n}/n+\delta_{\mu(w),n}+\|e\|_{L^{2}(P_{w})}^{2}). Minimize over deterministic f∗f^{*} and use treatment overlap to transfer the XX-only marginal-head error from PwP_{w} to PP: P​(f^−μ0)2≤Pr⁡(W=w)​Pw​(f^−μ0)2/ϵP(\hat{f}-\mu_{0})^{2}\leq\Pr(W=w)P_{w}(\hat{f}-\mu_{0})^{2}/\epsilon. Keep the outcome-head error under PwP_{w}, as in the definition of ρμ~​(w,⋅)\rho_{\tilde{\mu}(w,\cdot)}. This proves (10). The comparator may use a baseline encoder different from the fitted one because it belongs to the full class ℱm,w\mathcal{F}_{m,w}, while q^\hat{q} remains fixed in the empirical comparison. ∎

Outer cross-fitting separates nuisance fitting from score evaluation; it does not separate the outcome and marginal fits on the same training fold. The uniform bound handles that dependence, while the assumed final-fit optimization comparison supplies the otherwise missing marginal comparator.

G.3 Proof of Proposition 3

Proof.

Fix w∈{0,1}w\in\{0,1\}, and abbreviate qw⋆​(X,S)=μ~⋆​(w,X,S)q_{w}^{\star}(X,S)=\tilde{\mu}^{\star}(w,X,S) and q0​w​(X,S)=μ~0​(w,X,S)q_{0w}(X,S)=\tilde{\mu}_{0}(w,X,S). Conditional MAR gives

𝔼{R(Y−qw⋆)∣W=w,X,S}=r0(w,X,S)(q0​w−qw⋆).\mathbb{E}\{R(Y-q_{w}^{\star})\mid W=w,X,S\}=r_{0}(w,X,S)(q_{0w}-q_{w}^{\star}).

Indeed, 𝔼⁡(Y∣W=w,X,S,R=1)=q0​w\mathbb{E}(Y\mid W=w,X,S,R=1)=q_{0w} by definition, and 𝔼⁡(R​Y∣W=w,X,S)=r0​q0​w\mathbb{E}(RY\mid W=w,X,S)=r_{0}q_{0w}. Thus the conditional mean of the arm-ww correction in the score, given XX, is

𝔼[𝟏{W=w}ew⋆​(X){R⁡(Y−qw⋆)r⋆​(w,X,S)+qw⋆−μ⋆(w,X)}|X]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left.\frac{\mathbf{1}\{W=w\}}{e_{w}^{\star}(X)}\left\{\frac{R(Y-q_{w}^{\star})}{r^{\star}(w,X,S)}+q_{w}^{\star}-\mu^{\star}(w,X)\right\}\right|X\right]
=e0​w​(X)ew⋆​(X)𝔼[r0​(w,X,S)r⋆​(w,X,S)(q0​w−qw⋆)+qw⋆−μ⋆(w,X)|W=w,X].\displaystyle\quad=\frac{e_{0w}(X)}{e_{w}^{\star}(X)}\mathbb{E}\left[\left.\frac{r_{0}(w,X,S)}{r^{\star}(w,X,S)}(q_{0w}-q_{w}^{\star})+q_{w}^{\star}-\mu^{\star}(w,X)\right|W=w,X\right].

Write aw​(X)=e0​w​(X)/ew⋆​(X)a_{w}(X)=e_{0w}(X)/e_{w}^{\star}(X). Since μ0​w​(X)=𝔼⁡(q0​w∣W=w,X)\mu_{0w}(X)=\mathbb{E}(q_{0w}\mid W=w,X), the sum of μ⋆​(w,X)\mu^{\star}(w,X) and this correction, minus μ0​w​(X)\mu_{0w}(X), equals

μ⋆(w,X)−μ0​w(X)+aw𝔼[r0r⋆(q0​w−qw⋆)+qw⋆−μ⋆(w,X)|W=w,X]\displaystyle\mu^{\star}(w,X)-\mu_{0w}(X)+a_{w}\mathbb{E}\left[\left.\frac{r_{0}}{r^{\star}}(q_{0w}-q_{w}^{\star})+q_{w}^{\star}-\mu^{\star}(w,X)\right|W=w,X\right]
=(1−aw){μ⋆(w,X)−μ0​w(X)}+aw𝔼[(r0r⋆−1)(q0​w−qw⋆)|W=w,X].\displaystyle\quad=(1-a_{w})\{\mu^{\star}(w,X)-\mu_{0w}(X)\}+a_{w}\mathbb{E}\left[\left.\left(\frac{r_{0}}{r^{\star}}-1\right)(q_{0w}-q_{w}^{\star})\right|W=w,X\right].

Here r0/r⋆r_{0}/r^{\star} abbreviates the ratio evaluated at (w,X,S)(w,X,S). Under ignorability and conditional MAR, τ0=𝔼⁡{μ01​(X)−μ00​(X)}\tau_{0}=\mathbb{E}\{\mu_{01}(X)-\mu_{00}(X)\}. Taking expectations of the last display and subtracting the control-arm expression from the treated-arm expression proves (9). In each arm, either equality in the first displayed pair makes its first product zero, and either equality in the second pair makes its second product zero, proving the sufficient condition. ∎

G.4 Proof of Theorem 2

Proof.

Write s=scomps=s_{\mathrm{comp}} and take mm sufficiently large. Apply the bounded-weight approximation construction of Schmidt-Hieber (2020, Theorem 5) to each coordinate of b0b_{0}, each coordinate of g0g_{0}, and all seven representation-level heads. For every component vv of input dimension DvD_{v} and smoothness pvp_{v}, use grid size N=mN=m and accuracy parameter t=⌈(1+s)​log2​m⌉t=\lceil(1+s)\log_{2}m\rceil. Since pv/Dv≥sp_{v}/D_{v}\geq s, the construction gives a sup-norm error bounded by

C{m2−t+m−pv/Dv}=O(m−s)C\{m2^{-t}+m^{-p_{v}/D_{v}}\}=O(m^{-s})

with O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m) depth and O⁡(m​log⁡m)O(m\log m) active parameters. The coordinate changes from [−1,1][-1,1] to [0,1][0,1] only affect constants. Clip the approximated encoder coordinates to [−1,1][-1,1], the outcome heads to [−M,M][-M,M], and the probability heads to intervals within the true overlap bounds. Since the corresponding true components lie in these intervals, clipping cannot increase their approximation errors. The true encoder and head maps are Lipschitz on their compact domains because their Sobolev orders are at least one. For example, with b^m,g^m,q^w,m\hat{b}_{m},\hat{g}_{m},\hat{q}_{w,m} denoting the approximants of b0,g0,μ~0​(w,⋅)b_{0},g_{0},\tilde{\mu}_{0}(w,\cdot), respectively,

‖q^w,m​(b^m​(X),g^m​(b^m​(X),S))−μ~0​(w,X,S)‖∞\displaystyle\|\hat{q}_{w,m}(\hat{b}_{m}(X),\hat{g}_{m}(\hat{b}_{m}(X),S))-\tilde{\mu}_{0}(w,X,S)\|_{\infty}
≤‖q^w,m−μ~¯0​(w,⋅)‖∞+C​‖g^m−g0‖∞+C​‖b^m−b0‖∞=O⁡(m−s).\displaystyle\quad\leq\|\hat{q}_{w,m}-\bar{\tilde{\mu}}_{0}(w,\cdot)\|_{\infty}+C\|\hat{g}_{m}-g_{0}\|_{\infty}+C\|\hat{b}_{m}-b_{0}\|_{\infty}=O(m^{-s}).

The same triangle inequality applies to the other six composite heads. This constructs one shared encoder with all heads simultaneously close to their true composite nuisances; it does not claim that fitted encoder coordinates converge to these particular approximants. Because the number of components is fixed, parallelizing the component constructions and synchronizing their depths with bounded-weight ReLU identity modules yields a common layered architecture on (X,S)(X,S) with O⁡(log⁡m)O(\log m) depth and width O⁡(m)O(m) containing joint approximants with O⁡(m​log⁡m)O(m\log m) nonzero bounded weights and sup-norm error O⁡(m−s)O(m^{-s}) for each output. Restrict the joint sieve to at most O⁡(m​log⁡m)O(m\log m) nonzero parameters in this architecture; the support may vary across functions. It has W=O⁡(m2​log⁡m)W=O(m^{2}\log m) available parameter slots, but only sm=O⁡(m​log⁡m)s_{m}=O(m\log m) of them may be nonzero.

Apply the sparse bound of Lemma 5 on the bounded original input domain with L=O⁡(log⁡m)L=O(\log m), W=O⁡(m2​log⁡m)W=O(m^{2}\log m), sm=O⁡(m​log⁡m)s_{m}=O(m\log m), fixed parameter bound BB, and δ=1/n\delta=1/n. For polynomial mm, it gives log covering number O⁡(m​(log⁡n)3)O(m(\log n)^{3}) for each composite head. A product cover of the five supervised heads has the same order because their number is fixed. The two head covers in Lemma 7 also have this order.

To apply the joint comparison, let ℛsup\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{sup}} be the population version of ℛ^sup\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{sup}} in (7): its outcome term is conditional on R=1R=1, while its propensity terms use the full observed-data law. =λY​𝔼​[(μ~θ​(W,X,S)−μ~0​(W,X,S))2∣R=1]\displaystyle=\lambda_{Y}\mathbb{E}[(\tilde{\mu}_{\theta}(W,X,S)-\tilde{\mu}_{0}(W,X,S))^{2}\mid R=1]
+λR𝔼[KL{Bern(r0(W,X,S))∥Bern(rθ(W,X,S))}]\displaystyle\quad+\lambda_{R}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\operatorname{KL}\{\operatorname{Bern}(r_{0}(W,X,S))\|\operatorname{Bern}(r_{\theta}(W,X,S))\}\right]

The common approximant constructed above has population supervised excess risk O⁡(m−2​s)O(m^{-2s}): the squared-loss term is quadratic, and Bernoulli KL has bounded curvature on the clipping interval. For the joint class, the localized squared-loss and bounded cross-entropy arguments of Lemma 6 apply to the weighted sum of loss differences. Its variance is bounded by a constant times the population supervised excess risk, and the product-cover entropy is O⁡(m​(log⁡n)3)O(m(\log n)^{3}). The labeled sample count is of order nn in probability by positivity; conditioning on this count handles the normalization of the labeled squared-loss term. |{ℛ^sup​(θ)−ℛ^sup​(𝜼0)}−Δ⁡(θ)|≤14​Δ​(θ)+C​m​(log⁡n)3n.\left|\{\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{sup}}(\theta)-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathrm{sup}}(\bm{\eta}_{0})\}-\Delta(\theta)\right|\leq\tfrac{1}{4}\Delta(\theta)+C\frac{m(\log n)^{3}}{n}.

Thus the sum of squared errors of the five supervised nuisances has this bound, without asserting separate empirical optimality for any supervised head.

Lemma 5 applied to the composite outcome and marginal classes on (X,S)(X,S) gives Tn=O⁡(m​(log⁡n)3)T_{n}=O(m(\log n)^{3}). Lemma 7 and the already established outcome-head rate thus imply

ρμ⁡(w,⋅)2=OP​(m−2​s+m​(log⁡n)3n+δμ⁡(w),n+δsup,n).\rho_{\mu(w,\cdot)}^{2}=O_{P}\!\left(m^{-2s}+\frac{m(\log n)^{3}}{n}+\delta_{\mu(w),n}+\delta_{\mathrm{sup},n}\right).

With m≍(n/(log⁡n)3)1/(2​s+1)m\asymp(n/(\log n)^{3})^{1/(2s+1)} and s>1/2s>1/2, both the approximation and entropy terms are o(n−1/2)o(n^{-1/2}). If the two optimization gaps are also oP(n−1/2)o_{P}(n^{-1/2}), all seven nuisance errors are oP(n−1/4)o_{P}(n^{-1/4}), so the product-rate requirements of Theorem 1 follow.
